congo_square.name: Congo Square
congo_square.desc:
The open ground in New Orleans where enslaved and free Black people were permitted to gather, drum and dance through the early nineteenth century.

It is the clearest surviving link between West African rhythmic practice and the syncopation that later became jazz.

scott_joplin.name: Scott Joplin
scott_joplin.desc:
The leading composer of ragtime, whose published rags gave written form to syncopated American music around 1900.

Ragtime's left-hand stride and right-hand displacement became the piano vocabulary that early jazz players inherited and loosened.

buddy_bolden.name: Buddy Bolden
buddy_bolden.desc:
The New Orleans cornetist remembered as the first jazz bandleader, playing loud, blues-soaked improvisation in the years before 1907.

No recording of him survives, so his reputation rests entirely on the testimony of the musicians who heard him.

jelly_roll_morton.name: Jelly Roll Morton
jelly_roll_morton.desc:
Pianist, composer and self-mythologising showman who claimed to have invented jazz in 1902.

His Red Hot Peppers recordings are the first great arranged jazz records, balancing written ensemble parts against solo space.

king_oliver.name: King Oliver
king_oliver.desc:
Cornetist and leader of the Creole Jazz Band, the group that carried New Orleans polyphony north to Chicago in 1922 and made the first major recordings by Black jazz musicians.

His muted, vocalised cornet and his ensemble discipline set the template every early band worked from, with Lil Hardin at the piano and a second cornet chair he filled by sending home for the young Louis Armstrong.

He came up on the same hall-and-parade circuit as Kid Ory and Jelly Roll Morton, and lost his teeth, his band and his career to gum disease, dying as a pool-hall janitor in Savannah.

sidney_bechet.name: Sidney Bechet
sidney_bechet.desc:
The first great jazz soprano saxophonist, with a wide, urgent vibrato that dominated any ensemble he entered.

He was recorded as a soloist before Armstrong and spent his later career as a celebrated figure in France.

louis_armstrong.name: Louis Armstrong
louis_armstrong.desc:
The musician who turned jazz from a collective folk music into a soloist's art. The Hot Five and Hot Seven sides of 1925-28, organised by his wife Lil Hardin with Earl Hines answering him at the piano, proved a single improvising voice could carry a whole performance.

He learned cornet under King Oliver in New Orleans, took the lead chair when Oliver sent for him in Chicago, then spent a year with Fletcher Henderson in New York teaching that orchestra how to swing.

His phrasing, tone and singing went into everyone: Bessie Smith's records with him behind her, Billie Holiday's whole conception of the beat, and the trumpet line running through Eldridge and Gillespie to Wynton Marsalis.

lil_hardin_armstrong.name: Lil Hardin Armstrong
lil_hardin_armstrong.desc:
Pianist, arranger and bandleader who played in King Oliver's Creole Jazz Band and wrote and organised much of the Hot Five's material.

She pushed her husband to leave Oliver's band and stand as a soloist in his own right.

bix_beiderbecke.name: Bix Beiderbecke
bix_beiderbecke.desc:
Cornetist from Iowa whose cool, bell-clear tone offered an alternative to Armstrong's blazing attack.

His harmonic curiosity and early death at twenty-eight made him the first romantic legend of white jazz.

james_p_johnson.name: James P. Johnson
james_p_johnson.desc:
The father of Harlem stride piano, whose left hand turned ragtime's regularity into swinging propulsion.

He was the dominant figure in the New York rent-party scene and a serious composer of larger concert works.

fats_waller.name: Fats Waller
fats_waller.desc:
Stride pianist, organist and comic entertainer whose songs became jazz standards while his playing hid formidable technique behind a grin.

His records sold to audiences far outside the jazz public and kept the stride tradition popular into the swing era.

earl_hines.name: Earl Hines
earl_hines.desc:
The pianist who broke stride's rhythmic lockstep, playing single-note lines in octaves like a horn player.

His duets and band sides with Armstrong are among the most advanced jazz records of the 1920s, and his later big band incubated the first beboppers.

duke_ellington.name: Duke Ellington
duke_ellington.desc:
Bandleader and composer who treated his orchestra as an instrument, writing for the specific voices inside it — Hodges's glissando, Webster's breath — across half a century.

The Cotton Club residency from 1927 gave him a nightly laboratory and a radio wire; Billy Strayhorn's arrival in 1939 gave him a co-author whose hand is frequently impossible to separate from his own.

His catalogue is the largest body of composition in jazz, and the model of the composer-bandleader passed to Mingus, Sun Ra, Maria Schneider and the repertory programme Wynton Marsalis built at Lincoln Center.

count_basie.name: Count Basie
count_basie.desc:
Kansas City bandleader whose orchestra swung on riffs, space and the almost weightless pulse of the All-American Rhythm Section, with Jo Jones moving the beat onto the hi-hat.

He gave Lester Young the setting for the most influential tenor playing before Parker, and put the young Billie Holiday in front of the band for two years that clashing contracts kept off record.

His own piano grew sparer with age until a few placed notes could steer the whole orchestra — the opposite solution to Ellington's dense written colour, and the basis of a rivalry both men enjoyed.

billy_strayhorn.name: Billy Strayhorn
billy_strayhorn.desc:
Composer and arranger whose partnership with Ellington was so close that authorship of individual passages is often unrecoverable.

His own writing, harmonically lush and quietly melancholic, produced Take the A Train, Chelsea Bridge and Lush Life.

benny_goodman.name: Benny Goodman
benny_goodman.desc:
Clarinettist whose 1935 Palomar success is conventionally dated as the start of the swing craze.

He led racially integrated small groups in public at a time when that was commercially risky, and his precision set a technical standard for the era.

fletcher_henderson.name: Fletcher Henderson
fletcher_henderson.desc:
Bandleader and arranger who invented the big band language of answering brass and reed sections in the 1920s.

His charts, later sold to Benny Goodman, supplied the swing era with much of its written vocabulary.

coleman_hawkins.name: Coleman Hawkins
coleman_hawkins.desc:
The musician who made the tenor saxophone a jazz instrument, with a huge vertical sound built on running the chords.

His 1939 Body and Soul is a solo of almost pure harmony, and he stayed curious enough to hire the young beboppers.

lester_young.name: Lester Young
lester_young.desc:
Tenor player whose light tone and floating, behind-the-beat phrasing rejected everything Coleman Hawkins's vertical, chord-running style stood for; their Kansas City cutting contest split the instrument in two.

His solos with Basie between 1936 and 1940 are the most influential tenor playing before Parker, who learned them off records as a teenager, and his sides with Billie Holiday are the closest jazz gets to two voices completing each other's sentences.

He named her Lady Day and she named him Prez; she asked to sing at his funeral and was refused. Army imprisonment and drink wrecked him, and the melodic logic he invented passed into bebop and cool jazz regardless.

johnny_hodges.name: Johnny Hodges
johnny_hodges.desc:
Ellington's lead alto for four decades, with a gliding portamento that no one has convincingly copied.

He also led his own small groups, one of which briefly employed a young John Coltrane.

ben_webster.name: Ben Webster
ben_webster.desc:
Tenor saxophonist whose Ellington features paired a breathy, almost whispered ballad tone with a rasping attack on fast numbers.

He was the first major tenor voice in the Ellington orchestra and a model for later romantics on the instrument.

chick_webb.name: Chick Webb
chick_webb.desc:
Drummer and bandleader who ruled the Savoy Ballroom's battles of the bands from behind a custom kit.

Severely disabled by spinal tuberculosis, he played with a force that beat visiting orchestras on their own ground.

django_reinhardt.name: Django Reinhardt
django_reinhardt.desc:
Manouche guitarist who built a fluid single-line style using two fingers after a caravan fire damaged his left hand.

With the Quintette du Hot Club de France he proved that jazz could develop an original voice outside America.

mary_lou_williams.name: Mary Lou Williams
mary_lou_williams.desc:
Pianist and arranger who wrote for Kirk, Ellington, Goodman and Gillespie, and moved through every jazz style from stride to bebop without stalling.

Her Harlem apartment became the informal school where the young beboppers argued out their ideas.

jo_jones.name: Jo Jones
jo_jones.desc:
Basie's drummer, who shifted the pulse from the bass drum to the hi-hat and made swing rhythm float rather than thud.

That move freed the other limbs for accents and pointed directly at modern drumming.

roy_eldridge.name: Roy Eldridge
roy_eldridge.desc:
Trumpeter who bridged Armstrong and Gillespie, playing with saxophonic agility high in the register.

His time touring in white bands exposed him to humiliations that he spoke about with unusual bluntness.

charlie_christian.name: Charlie Christian
charlie_christian.desc:
The first great amplified guitarist, who gave the instrument a horn player's role in Goodman's small groups.

His after-hours playing at Minton's fed straight into bebop before tuberculosis killed him at twenty-five.

charlie_parker.name: Charlie Parker
charlie_parker.desc:
The alto saxophonist at the centre of bebop, who reorganised jazz around fast tempos, upper-interval harmony and an asymmetrical phrasing built out of Lester Young's melodic logic.

With Dizzy Gillespie he turned a set of after-hours discoveries at Minton's into a finished style, announced by the unison heads on Ko-Ko and Shaw Nuff; Art Tatum, heard nightly while Parker washed dishes in the same club, showed him what the passing chords could hold.

He hired the nineteen-year-old Miles Davis and was studied by Coltrane, Rollins, Adderley and Ornette Coleman. He died at thirty-four, leaving a language so complete that the next thirty years went on extending or escaping it.

dizzy_gillespie.name: Dizzy Gillespie
dizzy_gillespie.desc:
Trumpeter, composer and theorist who did more than anyone to codify bebop's harmony and teach it — where Parker discovered, Gillespie wrote down, explained and demonstrated.

He began as a Roy Eldridge imitator and inherited his chair, was fired by Cab Calloway after a spitball fight ended in a knife, and ran the Minton's bandstand using substitute changes to clear it of weaker players.

Hiring Chano Pozo in 1947 put genuine Afro-Cuban ritual drumming inside a jazz orchestra rather than a stylised imitation of it, permanently widening what jazz rhythm could contain.

thelonious_monk.name: Thelonious Monk
thelonious_monk.desc:
Pianist and composer whose angular tunes and deliberate dissonances stood apart from bebop even as he helped invent it on the Minton's bandstand as house pianist.

Mary Lou Williams sheltered and argued with him early, Coleman Hawkins hired him when the establishment thought him unplayable, and the 1957 Five Spot residency with Coltrane in the band turned him from cult figure into critical necessity.

His use of silence and displaced accent was dismissed as incompetence for years; Riverside eased him toward acceptance with albums of Ellington and standards before letting him record his own repertoire.

bud_powell.name: Bud Powell
bud_powell.desc:
The pianist who translated Parker's horn lines into a right-hand language, with the left hand reduced to sparse chordal jabs.

His career was repeatedly broken by institutionalisation and the after-effects of a police beating in 1945, and he was kept going in his last years largely by the patronage of others. He died in 1966 at forty-one.

max_roach.name: Max Roach
max_roach.desc:
Drummer who moved timekeeping to the ride cymbal and used the rest of the kit as a melodic voice.

He was also a political artist, whose We Insist! Freedom Now Suite tied jazz explicitly to the civil rights movement.

kenny_clarke.name: Kenny Clarke
kenny_clarke.desc:
The drummer who first shifted the beat to the cymbal and dropped bombs on the bass drum, inventing modern jazz time at Minton's.

He later settled in Paris and co-led the Clarke-Boland Big Band.

dexter_gordon.name: Dexter Gordon
dexter_gordon.desc:
Tall tenor player who married Hawkins's weight to Parker's line, phrasing far behind the beat with unhurried authority.

After fourteen years based in Europe, his 1976 return to New York was received as the homecoming of a lost tradition.

fats_navarro.name: Fats Navarro
fats_navarro.desc:
Trumpeter of extraordinary evenness and clarity, the bebop player whose sound was fat rather than piercing.

He died at twenty-six, leaving a small recorded legacy that shaped the next generation of brass players.

tadd_dameron.name: Tadd Dameron
tadd_dameron.desc:
The most lyrical composer-arranger of the bebop era, who wrote settings warm enough to carry the style's harshest harmony.

Tunes like Good Bait and If You Could See Me Now entered the standard repertoire.

j_j_johnson.name: J.J. Johnson
j_j_johnson.desc:
The trombonist who proved the slide could keep up with bebop tempos, playing with an accuracy listeners mistook for valves.

He was also a serious composer and later wrote extensively for film and television.

gil_evans.name: Gil Evans
gil_evans.desc:
Arranger who treated the orchestra as a field of colour, using French horn, tuba and flute to build textures a soloist could stand inside rather than in front of.

His partnership with Miles Davis ran from the Birth of the Cool nonet — assembled in his basement apartment with Mulligan, Konitz and John Lewis — through Miles Ahead, Porgy and Bess and Sketches of Spain.

Maria Schneider worked as his assistant copying scores in the eighties, which is how the approach survived him as a living practice rather than a style to be imitated from records.

gerry_mulligan.name: Gerry Mulligan
gerry_mulligan.desc:
Baritone saxophonist and arranger whose pianoless quartet showed how much counterpoint two horns could carry alone.

He wrote for the Birth of the Cool sessions and remained a fluent composer throughout his career.

chet_baker.name: Chet Baker
chet_baker.desc:
Trumpeter and singer whose vulnerable, vibratoless tone became the sound of West Coast jazz.

His career was repeatedly derailed by addiction, and his late European recordings are stark in a way the early ones are not.

lennie_tristano.name: Lennie Tristano
lennie_tristano.desc:
Blind pianist and severe teacher who built a school around long asymmetrical lines, rigorous ear training, and singing a solo through before playing it.

Lee Konitz studied with him for years and emerged with a pale, dry alto sound that was the only real alternative to Parker's vocabulary — Tristano's clearest mark on the music, and one made through a pupil rather than a record.

His 1949 free improvisations, cut with no agreed key or tempo, predate Ornette Coleman by a decade, though he rejected the label and spent his later life teaching rather than performing.

lee_konitz.name: Lee Konitz
lee_konitz.desc:
Alto saxophonist who found a way past Parker by playing pale, dry and endlessly variable lines.

He kept improvising against the same standards for seventy years, refusing to settle into a fixed vocabulary.

dave_brubeck.name: Dave Brubeck
dave_brubeck.desc:
Pianist who studied with Milhaud and brought block chords, polytonality and odd metres into a hugely popular quartet.

Time Out made 5/4 and 9/8 briefly into pop rhythms and became the first million-selling jazz album.

paul_desmond.name: Paul Desmond
paul_desmond.desc:
Alto saxophonist with a dry martini tone, as he described it, and a gift for melodic understatement.

He wrote Take Five and spent most of his career in Brubeck's quartet, providing its lyrical counterweight.

stan_getz.name: Stan Getz
stan_getz.desc:
Tenor player whose beautiful, breathy sound came directly out of Lester Young.

His bossa nova records with Jobim and Gilberto sold in enormous numbers and opened American ears to Brazilian music.

john_lewis.name: John Lewis
john_lewis.desc:
Pianist, composer and musical director of the Modern Jazz Quartet, who imported fugue and chamber restraint into jazz.

He championed the Third Stream idea that jazz and European composition could genuinely merge.

milt_jackson.name: Milt Jackson
milt_jackson.desc:
Vibraphonist whose slow-vibrato blues feeling supplied the heat that balanced the MJQ's formal cool.

Outside the quartet he was a hard-swinging blues player who recorded prolifically as a leader.

art_blakey.name: Art Blakey
art_blakey.desc:
Drummer whose press rolls and thunderous backbeat defined hard bop, and whose Jazz Messengers ran for thirty-five years as a finishing school with a paying audience.

He co-led the original band with Horace Silver, who supplied the gospel-inflected tunes; when Silver left with most of the personnel, Blakey kept the name and the method.

Lee Morgan, Bobby Timmons, Wayne Shorter, Freddie Hubbard, Keith Jarrett and finally Wynton Marsalis all passed through — joining as young players, writing for the band, and leaving as leaders.

horace_silver.name: Horace Silver
horace_silver.desc:
Pianist and composer who put gospel cadences and funky bass figures at the centre of the hard bop tune, with a right hand out of Bud Powell and the fury replaced by bounce.

He co-founded the Jazz Messengers with Art Blakey and then left with most of the band, spending nearly thirty years on Blue Note — longer than any other artist on the label.

Song for My Father gave Joe Henderson his most quoted solo, and the funky-tune tradition Silver established is where Herbie Hancock's Watermelon Man comes from.

clifford_brown.name: Clifford Brown
clifford_brown.desc:
Trumpeter of dazzling technique and warmth who stayed clear of the drug culture around him and was killed in a car crash at twenty-five, in the middle of his best work.

He took Fats Navarro's even, rounded tone as his model, and the quintet he co-led with Max Roach from 1954 is the archetype of the hard bop group: two virtuoso front-line voices over a drummer composing underneath them.

Lee Morgan inherited the succession in Philadelphia and Freddie Hubbard the sound, and no trumpeter since has worked entirely outside his shadow.

sonny_rollins.name: Sonny Rollins
sonny_rollins.desc:
Tenor saxophonist and the great thematic improviser, building solos by developing a motif rather than running changes.

He twice withdrew from public performance to practise alone, once for two years on the Williamsburg Bridge.

cannonball_adderley.name: Cannonball Adderley
cannonball_adderley.desc:
Alto saxophonist with a joyful, blues-drenched sound and a gift for talking an audience into the music.

His quintet made soul jazz commercially huge without thinning the harmonic content.

lee_morgan.name: Lee Morgan
lee_morgan.desc:
Trumpeter who joined Gillespie's band at eighteen and Blakey's at twenty, with a cocky, smeared attack all his own.

The Sidewinder became Blue Note's biggest seller; he was shot dead at a club at thirty-three.

wayne_shorter.name: Wayne Shorter
wayne_shorter.desc:
Saxophonist and composer whose tunes sidestep ordinary harmonic gravity, leaving the resolution implied rather than stated.

He wrote for Blakey, reshaped the second Miles quintet, co-founded Weather Report and led an open-form quartet into his eighties.

jimmy_smith.name: Jimmy Smith
jimmy_smith.desc:
The musician who made the Hammond B-3 a jazz instrument, walking basslines on the pedals while soloing above.

His Blue Note run created the organ trio format that filled Black neighbourhood clubs for two decades.

wes_montgomery.name: Wes Montgomery
wes_montgomery.desc:
Guitarist who played with his thumb instead of a pick, producing a round tone and a signature octave technique.

Self-taught from Charlie Christian records, he became the most imitated jazz guitarist of the century.

freddie_hubbard.name: Freddie Hubbard
freddie_hubbard.desc:
Trumpeter with a brilliant, aggressive tone who appeared on the key avant-garde records of the early sixties as easily as on hard bop dates.

His versatility took him from Ornette Coleman's Free Jazz to Blakey to seventies crossover.

jackie_mclean.name: Jackie McLean
jackie_mclean.desc:
Alto saxophonist with a deliberately sharp, crying pitch, who moved from Parker's language into free playing in the sixties.

He later built a major jazz education programme in Hartford and taught for thirty years.

miles_davis.name: Miles Davis
miles_davis.desc:
Trumpeter and bandleader at the centre of five revolutions — bebop, cool, hard bop, modal jazz and electric fusion — largely by hiring the right people and telling them what to leave out.

He joined Parker's quintet at nineteen, built the Birth of the Cool nonet with Gil Evans, took his sense of space from Ahmad Jamal, gave Coltrane and Bill Evans the modal frameworks of Kind of Blue, and assembled a second quintet in which Hancock, Carter and Williams could move the ground under a soloist mid-phrase.

Teo Macero cut the electric period into shape from hours of tape. The list of musicians who passed through his bands is close to a history of the music, and his argument with Wynton Marsalis over what he did after 1969 framed jazz's politics in the eighties.

john_coltrane.name: John Coltrane
john_coltrane.desc:
Tenor and soprano saxophonist whose development ran from dense chord-running to unmeasured free playing in fifteen years, an unusually public course of self-education.

Johnny Hodges gave him an apprenticeship, Miles Davis sacked him for unreliability in 1957 and later gave him the modal frameworks, and the 1957 Five Spot residency with Monk taught him to play through unfamiliar harmony rather than around it.

The quartet with McCoy Tyner, Elvin Jones and Jimmy Garrison produced A Love Supreme; his wife Alice replaced Tyner in 1966 and carried the devotional direction on after his death at forty. Kamasi Washington's generation still works from that last period.

bill_evans.name: Bill Evans
bill_evans.desc:
Pianist who rethought voicings around rootless chords and made the trio a conversation rather than a soloist with support.

His touch and harmonic sense passed into almost all subsequent jazz piano, and his life was shortened by long addiction.

ornette_coleman.name: Ornette Coleman
ornette_coleman.desc:
Alto saxophonist who removed the chord sequence and let melody, key and tempo move freely, calling the result harmolodics.

His 1959 New York engagement split the jazz world into supporters and enraged sceptics almost overnight.

cecil_taylor.name: Cecil Taylor
cecil_taylor.desc:
Pianist who treated the instrument as eighty-eight tuned drums, playing dense clusters at extreme sustained energy.

Conservatory-trained and fiercely articulate, he spent decades barely able to find paid work in America.

eric_dolphy.name: Eric Dolphy
eric_dolphy.desc:
Multi-instrumentalist on alto, bass clarinet and flute, whose leaping intervals sounded like speech to admirers and error to critics.

He died at thirty-six from undiagnosed diabetes while touring in Europe.

charles_mingus.name: Charles Mingus
charles_mingus.desc:
Bassist and composer who wrote collective, gospel-shouting, formally ambitious music and drilled it into his bands by ear at the piano, shouting from the bandstand as he went.

He took Ellington as his model for writing to individual players, and was famously fired from that orchestra within weeks; Eric Dolphy was the voice he wrote his most demanding parts for.

With Max Roach he founded Debut Records to own his own recordings and staged a rival festival against Newport in 1960. His work is openly political and openly autobiographical, and Esperanza Spalding's generation treats him as the model bassist-composer.

mccoy_tyner.name: McCoy Tyner
mccoy_tyner.desc:
Pianist whose stacked fourths and hammering left hand gave the Coltrane quartet its harmonic ground.

That voicing style became the default modal piano language for everyone who came after.

elvin_jones.name: Elvin Jones
elvin_jones.desc:
Drummer who played in overlapping triplet waves rather than a stated beat, surrounding the soloist instead of marking time.

His interaction with Coltrane is the most sustained duel in the music's recorded history.

jimmy_garrison.name: Jimmy Garrison
jimmy_garrison.desc:
Bassist who anchored the Coltrane quartet with a heavy, insistent pulse and long strummed solo passages.

His willingness to hold ground while the music around him dissolved made the group's freedom possible.

albert_ayler.name: Albert Ayler
albert_ayler.desc:
Tenor saxophonist who played hymns, marches and folk melodies through an enormous vibrato and shredded overtones.

His music was received as noise or as ecstasy, and his death in the East River at thirty-four remains unexplained.

sun_ra.name: Sun Ra
sun_ra.desc:
Pianist, bandleader and cosmic philosopher who claimed Saturn as his origin and ran the Arkestra as a communal discipline for decades.

He moved from Fletcher Henderson arrangements to early synthesisers without ever seeming to change direction.

archie_shepp.name: Archie Shepp
archie_shepp.desc:
Tenor saxophonist, playwright and academic who tied free jazz to Black liberation politics in print as well as in sound.

His playing keeps a rough, blues-rooted tone even at its most abstract.

don_cherry.name: Don Cherry
don_cherry.desc:
Pocket trumpeter who was Ornette Coleman's foil before becoming one of the first genuine world-music travellers in jazz.

His later work absorbed Turkish, Indian and Malian material long before that was fashionable.

alice_coltrane.name: Alice Coltrane
alice_coltrane.desc:
Pianist, harpist and composer who joined her husband's last band and then built a devotional music of her own from strings, harp and drone.

She later led an ashram in California and recorded chiefly for its community.

paul_chambers.name: Paul Chambers
paul_chambers.desc:
Bassist on an implausible number of the essential records of the fifties, from Kind of Blue to Blue Train.

He brought arco solos into the modern rhythm section and died at thirty-three.

philly_joe_jones.name: Philly Joe Jones
philly_joe_jones.desc:
Drummer of the first great Miles Davis quintet, whose crisp rimshot accents Davis described as the thing that made the band.

He combined bebop precision with a showman's sense of drama.

herbie_hancock.name: Herbie Hancock
herbie_hancock.desc:
Pianist and composer who has moved from Blue Note hard bop through the second Miles Davis quintet into funk, electronics and hip-hop, treating each idiom as a full commitment rather than a visit.

Donald Byrd gave him his first New York job, housed him and pushed Blue Note into signing him; Davis then taught him to comp less and imply more, and later handed him electric keyboards he had no wish to play.

Maiden Voyage, Head Hunters and Rockit each sound native to their moment, and Robert Glasper's jazz-and-hip-hop work is built explicitly on the precedent.

tony_williams.name: Tony Williams
tony_williams.desc:
Drummer who joined Miles Davis at seventeen and immediately dismantled the fixed beat, playing time as an elastic suggestion.

His Lifetime trio was one of the first genuinely loud jazz-rock groups.

ron_carter.name: Ron Carter
ron_carter.desc:
Bassist of the second Miles Davis quintet and the most recorded bassist in jazz history.

His note choice steers harmony rather than merely supporting it, opening space the rest of the band moves into.

chick_corea.name: Chick Corea
chick_corea.desc:
Pianist and composer who played electric piano in Davis's Bitches Brew bands and then founded Return to Forever.

He kept a parallel acoustic career, with Spanish and Latin material threaded through everything he wrote.

joe_zawinul.name: Joe Zawinul
joe_zawinul.desc:
Austrian keyboardist who wrote Mercy, Mercy, Mercy for Cannonball Adderley and then built Weather Report's sound out of layered synthesisers.

He was among the first to treat the synthesiser as an orchestral instrument rather than a novelty.

john_mclaughlin.name: John McLaughlin
john_mclaughlin.desc:
British guitarist whose speed and distortion on In a Silent Way and Bitches Brew helped define electric jazz.

With the Mahavishnu Orchestra and later Shakti he pushed jazz into odd metres and Indian classical structure.

jaco_pastorius.name: Jaco Pastorius
jaco_pastorius.desc:
Electric bassist who removed the frets from his instrument and played it as a singing lead voice, with harmonics, chords and a tone nobody had heard before.

He introduced himself to Weather Report by announcing that he was the greatest bass player in the world, then spent five albums justifying it; he also played on Mingus's last record and behind Joni Mitchell.

The claim he inherited from Scott LaFaro — that the bass may interrupt and carry melody — he made permanent, and Esperanza Spalding's generation plays inside it. Mental illness and homelessness ended his life at thirty-five.

weather_report.name: Weather Report
weather_report.desc:
The band Joe Zawinul and Wayne Shorter co-led from 1970 to 1986, founded on a stated principle that everybody soloed and nobody soloed.

It is the rare case of two established leaders agreeing to share one identity: Zawinul's layered synthesisers supplied the surface and pulled the group from abstract collective texture toward the funk of Heavy Weather, while Shorter largely subordinated his own voice to the ensemble.

Jaco Pastorius talked his way in during 1976 and turned the fretless bass into a lead instrument, which made the band a commercial force as well as a critical one.

keith_jarrett.name: Keith Jarrett
keith_jarrett.desc:
Pianist who played electric keyboards for Miles Davis while loathing them, then built a career on wholly improvised solo concerts.

The Koln Concert became the best-selling solo piano record ever made, and his standards trio ran for thirty years.

billie_holiday.name: Billie Holiday
billie_holiday.desc:
Singer who phrased like a horn player, bending the beat and the melody until a banal lyric became a statement of fact.

Bessie Smith and Louis Armstrong were her two stated sources; Teddy Wilson organised the 1935-39 studio sessions that produced her finest records, and Lester Young's obbligatos on them are the closest thing in jazz to a conversation between equals.

In 1939 she began performing Strange Fruit, Abel Meeropol's protest song about the lynching of Black Americans in the South. She kept it in her act for the rest of her life at considerable cost, and federal narcotics agents pursued her for years afterwards. Her late Verve sessions for Norman Granz catch a damaged voice with the phrasing intact.

ella_fitzgerald.name: Ella Fitzgerald
ella_fitzgerald.desc:
Singer of flawless intonation and the finest scat improviser in the music, able to trade choruses with any horn on the stand.

She won the Apollo amateur night in 1934 at seventeen having intended to dance, was hired by Chick Webb, and took over his orchestra when he died five years later — an almost unheard-of position for a woman of twenty-two.

Norman Granz then managed her for decades and built Verve around her, conceiving the Songbook series that fixed the American standard repertoire in place. Her duet albums with Armstrong run on the contrast between her precision and his rasp.

sarah_vaughan.name: Sarah Vaughan
sarah_vaughan.desc:
Singer with an operatic range and a bebopper's harmonic ear, developed while working alongside Parker and Gillespie in Earl Hines's and Billy Eckstine's bands.

She won the Apollo amateur night in 1942, which led straight to the Hines job; her 1945 sessions with Parker and Gillespie behind her put a bebop front line behind a popular singer for the first time.

She treated a standard as raw material for reharmonisation rather than a text to be delivered — the point on which she and her friend Carmen McRae diverged, and the source of the endless comparisons with Ella Fitzgerald.

nat_king_cole.name: Nat King Cole
nat_king_cole.desc:
Pianist of real distinction whose trio format influenced a generation before his singing made him a pop star.

His crossover success bought him a television show that sponsors refused to support.

betty_carter.name: Betty Carter
betty_carter.desc:
Singer who took standards at extreme tempos and stretched them past recognition, treating the voice as an improvising instrument.

She ran her own label and her trio functioned as a school for young pianists and drummers.

abbey_lincoln.name: Abbey Lincoln
abbey_lincoln.desc:
Singer, actress and songwriter who abandoned supper-club glamour for explicitly political material in the early sixties.

Her wordless screaming on the Freedom Now Suite is among the most confrontational moments on any jazz record.

blue_note_records.name: Blue Note Records
blue_note_records.desc:
The label Alfred Lion founded in 1939 and ran on the principle that musicians should be paid to rehearse before recording, which is why its sessions sound composed rather than assembled.

Rudy Van Gelder engineered nearly all of it and Reid Miles designed the covers; the fifties and sixties catalogue — Blakey, Silver, Monk, Morgan, Mobley, Shorter, Hancock, Jimmy Smith — is the central document of hard bop.

It recorded Monk and Cecil Taylor when nobody was buying, and its revivals with Cassandra Wilson and then Robert Glasper repeated the pattern of backing musicians slightly ahead of the market.

alfred_lion.name: Alfred Lion
alfred_lion.desc:
German emigre who founded Blue Note after hearing a Carnegie Hall boogie-woogie concert in 1938.

His insistence on paid rehearsal time is the practical reason Blue Note sessions sound rehearsed rather than assembled.

rudy_van_gelder.name: Rudy Van Gelder
rudy_van_gelder.desc:
Optometrist turned recording engineer who cut thousands of sessions, first in his parents' living room and then in a purpose-built studio in Englewood Cliffs.

The close, present piano and horn sound of postwar jazz is largely his.

columbia_records.name: Columbia Records
columbia_records.desc:
The major label that gave jazz musicians budgets and distribution far beyond the independents' reach.

Its jazz roster carried Ellington, Brubeck, Davis and later Wynton Marsalis to a mass audience.

teo_macero.name: Teo Macero
teo_macero.desc:
Columbia producer and composer who treated tape as a compositional medium, splicing hours of studio jamming into finished records.

Bitches Brew exists in its released form because of his editing as much as anyone's playing.

impulse_records.name: Impulse! Records
impulse_records.desc:
The label that branded itself the house that Trane built, packaging avant-garde jazz in gatefold orange and black.

It gave free players commercial release at a moment when almost no one else would.

minton_playhouse.name: Minton's Playhouse
minton_playhouse.desc:
The Harlem club whose after-hours sessions in the early 1940s functioned as bebop's laboratory, with a house band led by Kenny Clarke and Thelonious Monk at the piano.

The substitute chords and unreasonable tempos served a practical purpose: they cleared the stand of players who could not follow, which is how a jam session became a school.

Charlie Christian kept an amplifier there and played nightly after his Goodman gigs, and the amateur recordings made on the premises are the earliest surviving documents of the style forming.

cotton_club.name: Cotton Club
cotton_club.desc:
The Harlem venue that presented Black performers to a whites-only clientele through the Prohibition years.

Its radio broadcasts made Ellington nationally famous while its door policy showed exactly what the era's terms were.

village_vanguard.name: Village Vanguard
village_vanguard.desc:
The basement club on Seventh Avenue South, open since 1935 and still the most recorded room in jazz.

Its wedge-shaped acoustics turn up on live albums by Coltrane, Evans and dozens of others.

birdland.name: Birdland
birdland.desc:
The Broadway club named for Charlie Parker and billed as the jazz corner of the world.

Its nightly radio broadcasts carried the sound of bebop and early hard bop across America.

savoy_ballroom.name: Savoy Ballroom
savoy_ballroom.desc:
Harlem's integrated dance hall, with two bandstands so the music never stopped and a floor that drove the swing era's tempos.

The Lindy Hop was developed there, and the band battles it staged were treated as sporting events.

norman_granz.name: Norman Granz
norman_granz.desc:
Impresario who built Jazz at the Philharmonic and the Verve label, and wrote non-segregation clauses into his touring contracts.

He paid musicians properly and recorded them at length, which is why so much of the fifties survives on tape.

wynton_marsalis.name: Wynton Marsalis
wynton_marsalis.desc:
Trumpeter and composer who arrived in 1980 with classical and jazz credentials, a Blue Note-era vocabulary and a firm argument about what the tradition permits.

He joined Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers in 1980 as the last of that band's young leaders, was signed by Columbia as both a jazz and a classical artist, and built Jazz at Lincoln Center from a summer series into a permanent orchestra with its own hall.

His attack on Miles Davis's electric period, and Davis's reply, defined the jazz argument of the eighties; his brother Branford took precisely the pop work Wynton refused.

jazz_at_lincoln_center.name: Jazz at Lincoln Center
jazz_at_lincoln_center.desc:
The programme founded in 1987 that gave jazz a resident orchestra, a repertory mission and eventually its own building.

Its canon-forming choices remain the most argued-over question in contemporary jazz institutions.

pat_metheny.name: Pat Metheny
pat_metheny.desc:
Guitarist whose bright, chorused tone and open melodic writing built one of the largest audiences in modern jazz.

He has moved between pastoral group records and outright noise projects without apparent difficulty.

brad_mehldau.name: Brad Mehldau
brad_mehldau.desc:
Pianist who brought contrapuntal independence and rock repertoire into the standard trio format.

His left hand often carries a second melodic line rather than accompaniment, a habit borrowed from classical practice.

esperanza_spalding.name: Esperanza Spalding
esperanza_spalding.desc:
Bassist, singer and composer who writes across jazz, art song and R&B and sings intricate lines while playing them, a combination with almost no precedent.

She works from Mingus's model of the bassist as composer and bandleader, and from Betty Carter's of the singer as improvising instrumentalist who trains her own rhythm section, inside the melodic freedom Jaco Pastorius won for the instrument.

Her 2011 Grammy for Best New Artist was the first won by a jazz musician, and her later records have moved steadily away from the format that earned it.

robert_glasper.name: Robert Glasper
robert_glasper.desc:
Pianist who built a working bridge between jazz harmony and hip-hop production, with the Experiment project as the meeting point.

Black Radio brought rappers and R&B singers onto a jazz label's flagship release.

kamasi_washington.name: Kamasi Washington
kamasi_washington.desc:
Los Angeles tenor saxophonist whose triple album The Epic arrived in 2015 with choir, strings and an unembarrassed sense of scale.

He works from the last Coltrane period and from Alice Coltrane's and Pharoah Sanders's devotional records, taking the ambition rather than the abrasiveness.

With the West Coast Get Down, and through Kendrick Lamar and Robert Glasper, he pulled a young hip-hop audience toward spiritual jazz at a moment when jazz was assumed to have lost it.

maria_schneider.name: Maria Schneider
maria_schneider.desc:
Composer and bandleader who studied with Gil Evans and extended his colouristic writing into long, through-composed pieces.

Her orchestra has kept large-ensemble jazz composition alive as a living form rather than a repertory exercise.

bessie_smith.name: Bessie Smith
bessie_smith.desc:
The Empress of the Blues and the highest-paid Black performer of the 1920s, whose Columbia records sold in the hundreds of thousands and helped keep that label solvent.

She delivered a lyric as testimony rather than performance, and her 1925 session with Louis Armstrong is the first great meeting of blues voice and jazz horn, each answering the other phrase for phrase.

Billie Holiday named Smith and Armstrong as her two sources, and the low, unhurried authority Smith established runs forward through singers like Cassandra Wilson.

kid_ory.name: Kid Ory
kid_ory.desc:
New Orleans trombonist whose tailgate style, sliding countermelody under the cornet, is the sound of the classic front line.

His band gave early work to Oliver and Armstrong, and he led the first Black New Orleans group known to have recorded.

art_tatum.name: Art Tatum
art_tatum.desc:
Pianist of such technique that other musicians treated him as a separate category, reharmonising standards at speed and in real time.

Almost blind from childhood, he worked mainly solo and in after-hours rooms where the audience was other players.

teddy_wilson.name: Teddy Wilson
teddy_wilson.desc:
Pianist of poised, evenly articulated elegance who directed the classic Billie Holiday small-group sessions.

His place in Benny Goodman's trio made him one of the first Black musicians to perform regularly with a white band in public.

benny_carter.name: Benny Carter
benny_carter.desc:
Alto saxophonist, trumpeter and arranger whose section writing taught the swing era how reeds should voice a chord.

His career ran from the 1920s into the 1990s, and he later broke the colour bar in Hollywood studio orchestras.

cab_calloway.name: Cab Calloway
cab_calloway.desc:
Bandleader and showman whose Cotton Club revues and hi-de-ho routines made him a national figure.

Behind the act was a well-paid, well-drilled orchestra that employed several of the musicians who went on to invent bebop.

sonny_stitt.name: Sonny Stitt
sonny_stitt.desc:
Alto and tenor saxophonist who spent a career being accused of copying Parker, a charge he answered by pointing out he had arrived at the same place independently.

He was a formidable competitive player, best documented in tenor battles with Gene Ammons.

chano_pozo.name: Chano Pozo
chano_pozo.desc:
Cuban percussionist and composer who joined Dizzy Gillespie's big band in 1947 and put authentic rumba drumming inside a jazz orchestra.

He was shot dead in a Harlem bar a year later, having permanently changed what jazz rhythm could include.

oscar_pettiford.name: Oscar Pettiford
oscar_pettiford.desc:
Bassist who carried Blanton's innovations into bebop and pioneered the cello as a jazz solo instrument.

He led the bands that bridged the swing and bebop generations, and wrote several tunes that entered the repertoire.

ahmad_jamal.name: Ahmad Jamal
ahmad_jamal.desc:
Pianist whose trio built its music from space, vamps and dynamics rather than continuous soloing, and who sold records in quantities the jazz press treated as evidence against him.

Miles Davis told his own pianists to study him, had Red Garland reproduce his voicings on demand, and took several tunes straight from his book — which makes Jamal one of the strongest influences on the most influential band of the fifties.

He worked in the same format for six decades, and the negative space he pioneered surfaces again in pianists like Robert Glasper.

hank_mobley.name: Hank Mobley
hank_mobley.desc:
Tenor saxophonist described as the middleweight champion of the horn, playing with a soft tone and unfailing rhythmic placement.

His long Blue Note run produced Soul Station, one of the most admired tenor records of the era.

grant_green.name: Grant Green
grant_green.desc:
Guitarist who played single lines with an almost vocal simplicity, avoiding chords for long stretches.

His later boogaloo and funk sessions became among the most heavily sampled records in hip-hop.

donald_byrd.name: Donald Byrd
donald_byrd.desc:
Trumpeter and educator who moved from hard bop through gospel choir experiments into outright funk with the Blackbyrds.

He built jazz programmes at several universities and treated teaching as equal in weight to playing.

bobby_timmons.name: Bobby Timmons
bobby_timmons.desc:
Pianist and composer whose gospel-drenched tunes gave soul jazz its biggest hits.

Moanin' and Dat Dere are so idiomatic that they are often assumed to be traditional rather than written.

joe_henderson.name: Joe Henderson
joe_henderson.desc:
Tenor saxophonist with a dry, flickering tone who could work inside hard bop, modal and free settings without changing his voice.

After years of undervaluation he became a major concert draw in the 1990s with a series of thematic albums.

red_garland.name: Red Garland
red_garland.desc:
Pianist of the first Miles Davis quintet, a former boxer whose block chords and light touch gave the band its relaxed surface.

His comping is the practical demonstration of what Davis wanted from a piano chair.

jimmy_cobb.name: Jimmy Cobb
jimmy_cobb.desc:
Drummer whose brushed and cymbal-led playing is the pulse of Kind of Blue, the only drummer on that session.

He worked steadily for six decades and outlived every other musician on the record.

scott_lafaro.name: Scott LaFaro
scott_lafaro.desc:
Bassist who abandoned the walking line for a conversational, counter-melodic role inside the Bill Evans trio.

He was killed in a car crash at twenty-five, days after the Village Vanguard recordings that document what he had found.

paul_motian.name: Paul Motian
paul_motian.desc:
Drummer who moved from the Evans trio through Keith Jarrett's American quartet into a late career of near-weightless free playing.

He treated pulse as something to imply rather than state, and led bands with no bassist at all.

pharoah_sanders.name: Pharoah Sanders
pharoah_sanders.desc:
Tenor saxophonist who joined Coltrane's last band and matched its intensity with overtone-shredded screams.

His own records pulled that energy back toward modal calm, and Karma became a touchstone of spiritual jazz.

anthony_braxton.name: Anthony Braxton
anthony_braxton.desc:
Saxophonist, composer and theorist whose diagrammatically titled works sit between free jazz and post-serial composition.

He recorded the first full album of solo saxophone improvisation and has taught for decades as a systematising thinker about the music.

aacm.name: AACM
aacm.desc:
The Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians, founded on Chicago's South Side in 1965 as a self-run collective with its own school and concerts.

It gave a generation of experimental Black musicians an alternative to the club and label economy.

jack_dejohnette.name: Jack DeJohnette
jack_dejohnette.desc:
Drummer of enormous breadth who played on Bitches Brew and then held Keith Jarrett's standards trio together for three decades.

He is also a pianist and composer, which is audible in how he tunes and voices the kit.

michael_brecker.name: Michael Brecker
michael_brecker.desc:
Tenor saxophonist who absorbed Coltrane's harmonic apparatus and applied it to funk, pop sessions and jazz-rock.

He became the most imitated tenor sound of the 1980s and one of the most recorded sidemen of any era.

george_benson.name: George Benson
george_benson.desc:
Guitarist of formidable bebop technique who became a pop star by singing in unison with his own solo lines.

The crossover success drew accusations of selling out that his playing on jazz dates comfortably answers.

cassandra_wilson.name: Cassandra Wilson
cassandra_wilson.desc:
Singer with a dark contralto who rebuilt the jazz vocal repertoire around blues, folk and rock material.

Blue Light 'Til Dawn replaced the standard rhythm section with acoustic guitars and hand percussion, and changed what a jazz vocal record could sound like.

carmen_mcrae.name: Carmen McRae
carmen_mcrae.desc:
Singer and pianist whose dry, ironic delivery treated a lyric as text to be interrogated rather than sold.

She came up as the intermission pianist at Minton's, married Kenny Clarke and recorded briefly as Carmen Clarke, and was a serious enough musician to close her career with a full album of Monk's tunes set to lyrics.

prestige_records.name: Prestige Records
prestige_records.desc:
The independent label that recorded much of the fifties in single unrehearsed sessions, on the principle that studio time cost money.

The method produced loose, blowing-date records that are historically invaluable and occasionally shambolic.

riverside_records.name: Riverside Records
riverside_records.desc:
The label that gave Monk his first properly promoted albums and built rosters around Bill Evans, Wes Montgomery and Cannonball Adderley.

Orrin Keepnews's production put an emphasis on repertoire and framing that Prestige rarely bothered with.

ecm_records.name: ECM Records
ecm_records.desc:
The Munich label founded in 1969 whose spacious, reverberant recorded sound became a style in itself.

It gave European and American improvisers a home for music too quiet or too abstract for the American majors.

five_spot_cafe.name: Five Spot Café
five_spot_cafe.desc:
The Bowery bar that became the room where the New York avant-garde was first heard, on a liquor licence and a battered piano.

Monk's 1957 residency with Coltrane in the band ran for months and made both men's reputations; Ornette Coleman's 1959 opening split the jazz world so completely that established musicians queued at the bar to denounce or defend him.

Cecil Taylor and Eric Dolphy also held residencies there, and the painters and poets from the surrounding blocks made up much of the audience.

newport_jazz_festival.name: Newport Jazz Festival
newport_jazz_festival.desc:
The festival founded in 1954 that moved jazz from clubs into open-air concerts and a mass summer audience.

Its commercial success and its programming choices have been contested by musicians since almost its first years.

apollo_theater.name: Apollo Theater
apollo_theater.desc:
The Harlem theatre whose Wednesday amateur nights and merciless audience functioned as the toughest audition in American music.

Most of the major jazz singers of the century passed its test or failed it in public.

branford_marsalis.name: Branford Marsalis
branford_marsalis.desc:
Saxophonist who moved between his brother's acoustic quartets, Sting's touring band and the Tonight Show, then built a long-running quartet of his own.

He has been notably less doctrinaire than Wynton about where the tradition's boundaries lie.

vijay_iyer.name: Vijay Iyer
vijay_iyer.desc:
Pianist and composer working from rhythmic structures drawn from South Indian music, hip-hop and mathematics.

He writes extensively about perception and rhythm and teaches at Harvard, treating theory and playing as one activity.

christian_mcbride.name: Christian McBride
christian_mcbride.desc:
Bassist of encyclopaedic reach who has recorded with everyone from Sonny Rollins and Chick Corea to James Brown, Sting and Pat Metheny.

He also runs festivals and broadcasts, occupying the role of jazz's public advocate in his generation.

irene_kitchings.name: Irene Kitchings
irene_kitchings.desc:
Pianist and songwriter, married to Teddy Wilson, who wrote a small number of songs of unusual harmonic depth for Billie Holiday.

She gave up performing after her marriage and is remembered mainly through other people's records, which is a reasonable summary of how the era treated women who wrote.

artie_shaw.name: Artie Shaw
artie_shaw.desc:
Clarinettist and bandleader who matched Benny Goodman commercially and disliked the whole business of being a bandleader, walking away from it repeatedly.

He hired Billie Holiday in 1938 and Roy Eldridge in 1944, then found himself fighting hotels, sponsors and radio networks over their presence on his stand.

nica_de_koenigswarter.name: Pannonica de Koenigswarter
nica_de_koenigswarter.desc:
Rothschild heiress who left a diplomatic marriage for the New York jazz scene and spent thirty years housing, feeding and bailing out musicians.

Charlie Parker died in her hotel suite, Thelonious Monk lived under her roof at the end, and she is the dedicatee of some sixty tunes — the most thanked non-musician in the music.

bruce_lundvall.name: Bruce Lundvall
bruce_lundvall.desc:
Record executive who signed Wynton Marsalis to Columbia in 1980 and then relaunched Blue Note in 1984, running it for nearly thirty years.

He worked on the principle that you sign the musician rather than the market, which produced both the young-lions boom and the label's later vocal successes.

mario_bauza.name: Mario Bauzá
mario_bauza.desc:
Cuban trumpeter and musical director who is the hinge between Afro-Cuban music and jazz, first in Chick Webb's band and then as Cab Calloway's director.

He got Dizzy Gillespie into the Calloway orchestra, introduced him to Chano Pozo, and co-founded Machito's Afro-Cubans, the band where the fusion was worked out in full.

links.details:
The drumming and dancing tolerated at Congo Square kept African rhythmic practice alive in New Orleans for generations.

Bolden's generation inherited that pulse and pushed it through brass band instrumentation.

Morton grew up a few streets from the square in a downtown Creole household, and the habanera bass figure he called the Spanish tinge belongs to the same Afro-Caribbean current the drumming there kept alive.
Bechet came out of the same downtown Creole New Orleans that surrounded the square, and the vocalised urgency of his playing draws on the ring-shout tradition preserved in it.
Morton learned the ragtime repertoire as a young pianist in the New Orleans districts, then claimed he had improved it by adding the Spanish tinge and loosening the rhythm.
Johnson learned the published rags note-perfect as a boy, then loosened Joplin's even eighths into the swinging stride left hand that Harlem danced to.
Oliver came up in the cornet succession Bolden started, inheriting both his role as loudest man in the city and the blues inflection that went with it.
Armstrong was a small child when Bolden was committed, but grew up on streets where Bolden's sound was still the measure against which every New Orleans cornetist was judged.

Oliver gave Armstrong his first cornet lessons in New Orleans, put work his way, and in 1922 sent for him to play second cornet in the Creole Jazz Band in Chicago — the summons that took Armstrong out of the South.

On the records they made together the two cornets play worked-out breaks in harmony, the pupil audibly holding himself below the teacher. It lasted two years: Lil Hardin pushed Armstrong to leave, and Oliver never had a comparable player again.
Hardin was the Creole Jazz Band's pianist, and it was in Oliver's band that she met the young second cornetist.

Hardin married Armstrong in 1924 and pushed him to leave Oliver's band, take the lead chair and record under his own name.

She organised and played on the Hot Five sessions that resulted.

Hines was the first pianist who could meet Armstrong on equal terms, playing single-note lines in octaves like a horn rather than keeping stride time under him.

Their 1928 duet Weather Bird is two soloists pushing each other with no rhythm section to hide behind, trading four-bar phrases that keep threatening to fall apart and never do. It is the earliest jazz record that sounds like a conversation between equals.
The two New Orleans men recorded together in the mid-twenties, and their competitive front-line playing exposes the difference between Bechet's vibrato-heavy attack and Armstrong's rhythmic poise.
Beiderbecke heard Armstrong on the riverboats and in Chicago, and built a deliberately cooler alternative on the same foundation.
Eldridge worked out the West End Blues cadenza as a young man and built his own high-register attack on Armstrong's rhythmic placement rather than his tone.
Gillespie called Armstrong the source of everything trumpeters do, even while the beboppers were publicly mocking his stage manner — a contradiction he later regretted in print.
Holiday said she wanted to sound like Armstrong's horn and Bessie Smith's voice at once, and took her phrasing behind the beat directly from his playing.

Their Verve duet albums set her precision against his rasp on the same standards, and the contrast is the entire point — she sings the song, he comments on it.

Granz produced them with a small rhythm section and no arrangements to speak of, which leaves the two voices exposed. Porgy and Bess apart, they are the most relaxed records either made.
Marsalis has spent his career arguing for Armstrong as the central figure of American music, and programmed his work extensively at Lincoln Center.

Armstrong's year in Henderson's New York orchestra in 1924-25 is the most consequential single hire in jazz. He arrived unable to read well and left having taught a whole band, including Coleman Hawkins, what swing felt like.

What he took in return was the discipline of written arrangement — how a soloist stands inside an orchestrated background — which is exactly what he applied on returning to Chicago for the Hot Five.

Two New Orleans men who made their reputations in Chicago in the same few years, recording for the same label with overlapping personnel while Morton insisted to anyone listening that his bands were the better organised.
Ellington dismissed Morton's playing in public but took from the Red Hot Peppers records the principle that a jazz band could be composed for rather than merely arranged.
Waller was Johnson's pupil in Harlem, learning the stride left hand at close quarters before turning it into a popular entertainment.
Ellington learned Johnson's Carolina Shout from a piano roll, slowing it down to follow the keys, and later met him in a Washington cutting contest.
Basie sat beside Waller at the organ in a Harlem theatre and learned the pedals from him, a debt audible in his later economy at the keyboard.
Cole's trio piano is built on Hines's horn-like right hand, and he was still playing that way on the sessions where his singing began to overtake his reputation.
Hines's habit of playing horn-like single lines in the right hand, breaking free of stride's fixed pattern, is the direct ancestor of bebop piano.

Parker spent 1943 in the Hines big band playing tenor rather than alto, alongside Gillespie and Sarah Vaughan.

The wartime recording ban means almost none of what that band was doing survives.
Young studied the light, unforced sound of the Beiderbecke and Trumbauer records and built his tenor tone against the prevailing heaviness.

Strayhorn arrived in 1939 with a set of directions Ellington had written on a napkin, wrote Take the A Train from them, and stayed until his death in 1967.

They worked so closely that authorship of individual passages is often unrecoverable, and Ellington made little effort to clarify it — a generosity and a theft at once, depending on who is telling it. Strayhorn's own writing, Chelsea Bridge and Lush Life, is more harmonically melancholy than anything Ellington wrote alone.
Ellington wrote features specifically for Hodges's glissando, and treated the alto chair as a fixed colour in his palette for four decades.
Webster's arrival in 1940 gave the orchestra its first major tenor voice, and the Blanton-Webster band is generally taken as Ellington's peak.

Two orchestras solving the same problem in opposite ways: Ellington's dense written colour against Basie's riffs, space and near-weightless rhythm section.

The rivalry was real and largely friendly, conducted through the press, the ballroom circuit and eventually a 1961 session that put both bands in one studio at once. Neither man attempted the other's method; each simply got better at his own.

Mingus took Ellington as his model for writing to individual players rather than to instruments, and said so constantly and loudly.

He also lasted a matter of weeks in the orchestra, fired after chasing Juan Tizol with a fire axe — an episode Ellington described with amusement. They met again on Money Jungle, a trio date with Max Roach that turns openly combative and sounds like nothing else in either catalogue.
Their 1962 meeting put Coltrane in Ellington's rhythmic world rather than the reverse, and Ellington refused to let him rework first takes.
Money Jungle set Ellington against Mingus and Roach in a trio that turned openly combative, which is why it still sounds unlike anything else in his catalogue.
Sun Ra took from Ellington the model of a permanent orchestra as a self-contained world, with costume, ceremony and a leader writing for named individuals rather than chairs.
Marsalis treats Ellington as the model of the composer-bandleader and has made his catalogue central to the Lincoln Center repertory.
Schneider works squarely in the Ellington-Strayhorn practice of writing to specific players, and has arranged his material for her own orchestra.
Transcribing and performing the Ellington catalogue was the programme's founding argument that jazz belonged in a concert hall with a repertory orchestra.
Williams wrote for the Ellington orchestra, and for Goodman and Kirk besides, one of very few arrangers to work across the era's rival bands.

Williams's Harlem apartment was where the young modernists gathered — she fed them, argued harmony with them and defended their music in print when the critics would not.

Monk was the one she took most seriously and stayed closest to. She was a generation older, had written for Kirk, Ellington and Goodman, and gave the beboppers the one thing they could not get from each other: an established professional's confirmation that they were not simply wrong.
Williams wrote In the Land of Oo-Bla-Dee and other charts for Gillespie's big band, one of very few swing-era arrangers the beboppers took seriously.
Powell was among the young pianists Williams fed, argued with and defended, and she stayed loyal to him after his health collapsed.

The residency from 1927 gave Ellington a floor show to write for, a band he could keep together, and a radio wire that carried him nationally.

The jungle-style writing he developed there — growl brass, Bubber Miley's plunger — was made to accompany a floor show staged for a whites-only audience, and he spent decades converting that commercial obligation into a serious body of composition.
Armstrong fronted the club's revues at the end of the thirties, by which point he was a national star being presented to the same segregated audience the room had always served.
Evans's transparent voicings owe much to Strayhorn's harmonic palette, and both men wrote as colourists rather than as arrangers of existing tunes.
Goodman bought Henderson's charts when Henderson's own band failed, and the swing era's biggest white success was played out of a Black arranger's book.
Hawkins spent a decade in Henderson's orchestra, arriving as a slap-tongue novelty player and leaving as the definitive jazz tenor.
Before Saturn, Sun Ra worked as pianist and arranger for Henderson's band in Chicago, which is why his Arkestra's writing keeps a swing-era backbone under the noise.

Hawkins ran the chords vertically with an enormous tone; Young played melodically, light and behind the beat. Their 1933 Kansas City cutting contest ran all night and became the founding legend of the instrument.

Every tenor player afterwards effectively chose a side: Rollins and Coltrane out of Hawkins, Getz and Konitz out of Young. The two men respected each other and rarely recorded together, which kept the argument abstract enough to last.
Rollins took Hawkins as his first model for tone and thematic development, and the two eventually recorded together in 1963.
Hawkins hired Monk in 1944 when the older swing establishment considered him unplayable, and gave him his first significant recording work.
Hawkins played on the Freedom Now Suite, lending the older generation's authority to Roach and Lincoln's civil rights statement.

Young's solos with Basie between 1936 and 1940 are the most influential tenor playing before Parker, and the band was built to make them possible: riffs behind him, space around him, and a rhythm section that never landed hard.

He left, returned, and left again after the Army broke him. The Basie years remain the recorded case for his whole conception of playing melody across the bar rather than inside it.
Jones held the drum chair from the Kansas City years to 1948, and the band's floating pulse is inseparable from his hi-hat.

With Walter Page and Freddie Green, Basie and Jones formed the All-American Rhythm Section — the unit that made swing float instead of stamp.

Jones moved timekeeping from the bass drum to the hi-hat, which freed the rest of the kit for accents and freed Basie to play almost nothing. The band's identity is a rhythmic one before it is a harmonic one, and it belongs to the four of them jointly.
Holiday toured with the band in 1937-38, a partnership that clashing record contracts kept almost entirely off disc — it survives in a handful of broadcast airchecks.
Jones moved timekeeping to the hi-hat and freed the bass drum; Roach completed the move by shifting to the ride cymbal and treating the kit melodically.

On the small-group sides of 1937-41 Young plays obbligatos behind Holiday that answer her phrasing rather than decorate it, both of them singing slightly behind the beat.

He named her Lady Day; she named him Prez. They were close, then estranged for years, and met again in 1957 on the television broadcast The Sound of Jazz, where a frail Young played one chorus of Fine and Mellow with Holiday watching him — the last time either was captured at full strength.

She asked to sing at his funeral in March 1959 and was refused. She died four months after him.

Parker learned Young's Basie solos note for note off records as a teenager in Kansas City, playing them until he could reproduce them in any key.

What he took was not the tone, which he never imitated, but the principle of building long asymmetrical melodic lines that ignore the bar line. Bebop's rhythmic freedom starts there, which is why Young is the pivot on which the swing era turns into the modern one.
Getz built his tone out of Young's lightness so closely that some of his early sides were mistaken for the older man's.
Konitz treated Young's long unaccented lines as proof that an alto player could find a way past Parker rather than through him.
Webb's band was the Savoy's house orchestra and rarely lost a battle there, including the 1937 meeting with Benny Goodman's band.
Goodman's orchestra played the Savoy repeatedly, most famously in the May 1937 battle with Chick Webb that the Harlem crowd scored against him.
Fitzgerald spent her first professional years on the Savoy stage with Webb's band, singing for dancers rather than for listeners.

Webb hired Fitzgerald at seventeen straight out of the Apollo amateur night, and had to be persuaded — she was unpolished and looked unpresentable on a bandstand.

She became the band's main attraction within two years, and when he died in 1939 she took the orchestra over and fronted it for three more. The relationship is the clearest case in swing of an established leader building a successor rather than a sideman.
The Savoy band battles between the two orchestras were reported like prizefights, and Webb's home-floor victories became part of Harlem's folklore.
Goodman was talked into auditioning Christian, then built his sextet around the amplified guitar, giving the instrument its first solo platform in a major band.
Montgomery learned Christian's recorded solos note for note before he could read music, and played them on gigs as his entire early repertoire.
Christian knew the Quintette records and took from them the idea of the guitar as a single-line solo voice rather than a rhythm instrument.
Montgomery's habit of building a solo in stages, single notes to octaves to block chords, owes as much to Reinhardt's dramatic pacing as to Christian's line.
McLaughlin cites Reinhardt as the first evidence that a European could invent something in jazz rather than merely reproduce it.

Gillespie began as an outright Eldridge imitator, learned his solos, and then took his chair in Teddy Hill's band — the succession made literal.

He only found his own voice by pushing Eldridge's saxophone-like agility into harmony Eldridge had no interest in. The two remained close, and Eldridge's later view was that the young men had gone somewhere he could see clearly and did not want to follow.
Granz made Eldridge a fixture of Jazz at the Philharmonic and recorded him for Clef and Verve at the point when the swing generation was otherwise being dropped by the labels.
Coltrane spent 1954 in Hodges's small band, an unglamorous apprenticeship that gave him a direct line back to the Ellington tradition.
Shepp kept Webster's breathy, rasping ballad tone at the centre of his sound, which is why even his freest playing stays audibly rooted in the swing tenor tradition.

Monk was house pianist at Minton's in the early forties, where the substitute harmony he was working out became one of bebop's foundations.

The club paid badly and mattered enormously: a Monday-night stage with a house band that could set the tempo and the changes, and a policy of using both to embarrass unprepared sitters-in. Everything Monk later became recognisable for was already in place there, and largely ignored.

Clarke led the house band and used the sessions to test moving the pulse onto the ride cymbal and dropping bombs on the bass drum — a change the older players heard as an inability to keep time.

He had been fired from Teddy Hill's band for exactly that, and Hill then hired him to run Minton's. Modern jazz drumming was worked out on a Harlem bandstand by a man whose method had already cost him a job.
Gillespie worked out substitute chord changes on the Minton's bandstand and used them to run less capable sitters-in off the stage.
Parker sat in at Minton's and at Monroe's during his early New York years, and the musicians who were listening carried the news of what he was doing.

Christian kept an amplifier at Minton's and played there nightly after finishing with Benny Goodman, which is how the era's best-paid guitarist ended up inventing a style for free.

The amateur discs Jerry Newman cut on the premises are the earliest surviving documents of bebop forming, and Christian is the clearest voice on them. He was dead of tuberculosis at twenty-five, before any of it was released.

Parker and Gillespie played unison heads at tempos nobody else could hold, and the 1945 sides — Salt Peanuts, Shaw Nuff, Ko-Ko — announced bebop as a finished style rather than an experiment.

The division of labour was clear: Parker discovered, Gillespie organised, wrote it down and taught it. The partnership survived a disastrous Los Angeles residency, Parker's collapse, and years of mutual irritation, and both regarded the other as the only real peer available.

Davis joined the quintet at nineteen, knew he could not match Parker's speed, and built an economical middle-register style instead — the limitation that became his identity.

He also spent two years handling a leader who pawned instruments and vanished before sets, which taught him a great deal about how not to run a band. He said afterwards that everything he knew about music he learned in that group.
Roach was the drummer on most of the classic quintet sessions, learning to place accents behind a soloist who never phrased in even bars.
Powell was the pianist at the 1953 Massey Hall concert and on several Parker sessions, the one accompanist whose right hand could match him.
Their surviving Royal Roost broadcasts catch the two trading at length, and are the best evidence of how Navarro handled Parker's tempos.

Parker and Gillespie played behind Vaughan on her 1945 sessions, including Lover Man, putting a bebop front line behind a popular singer for the first time.

She had come up with both of them in Earl Hines's and Billy Eckstine's bands and could hear the harmony they were using, which is why the records work as jazz rather than as novelty. Her willingness to reharmonise a standard dates from there.
McLean grew up near Parker in New York, was lent horns and instruction by him, and spent his early career being told he sounded like a copy.
Rollins was a teenage Parker disciple in Harlem, and Parker's evident disappointment at finding him using heroin was part of what made him stop.
Gordon carried Parker's phrasing onto the tenor at a slower, heavier gait, becoming the model for how the larger horn could play bebop without scrambling.
Adderley arrived in New York in 1955 and was immediately labelled the new Bird, a comparison he spent years playing around rather than into.

Coltrane heard Parker in 1945 and described it as a permanent reorganisation of what he understood music to be.

His early tenor playing is an attempt to get an alto vocabulary onto the larger horn, and the running of chords that became sheets of sound starts as Parker's method taken past the point Parker used it. He kept the debt explicit and later recorded with Parker's rhythm section players.
Coleman started inside Parker's language and concluded that the chord sequences underneath it were the part that could be discarded.
Mingus measured everyone against Parker and wrote several pieces as open memorials, including one titled to make the debt unmissable.
Parker hired the young Baker for West Coast dates in 1952, which is what made his name before the Mulligan quartet.
Granz recorded Parker with strings and in the Jazz at the Philharmonic jam sessions, giving him both a commercial vehicle and steady touring money.
The club was named after him in 1949, and he was later barred from the premises during his decline.
Davis worked the club through the fifties, and was beaten by police outside it in 1959 while standing on the pavement between sets.
The Basie band was Birdland's most frequent big-band draw, and the nightly broadcasts from the club carried his postwar orchestra across the country.
Vaughan was among the singers the club built its bills around, backed by whichever bebop rhythm section was in residence that week.
Coltrane played in Gillespie's big band and then his small group in the early fifties, where he was still an unremarkable section player.
Johnson played in Gillespie's big band, where the trombone section had to negotiate bebop lines written with no regard for the slide.
The two worked out the new relationship between horn and drums at Minton's, and Clarke remained Gillespie's first-choice drummer for years.
Morgan joined Gillespie's big band at eighteen, straight out of Philadelphia, and was given the lead trumpet features almost immediately.
Davis came to New York looking for Gillespie as much as Parker, and was told to stop straining for the high register and find a sound of his own.
Both were in Billy Eckstine's band, and Gillespie's obbligatos on her early sessions set the pattern for how a bebop horn frames a singer.
Dameron wrote for the Gillespie big band, supplying ensemble settings lush enough to make the harmony palatable to dancers.
Dameron's band gave Navarro his most sympathetic setting, pairing bebop lines with warm ensemble writing rather than bare rhythm section.

Brown took Navarro's fat, even tone and unhurried articulation as his starting point, and the resemblance is close enough that the two are confused on blindfold tests.

Navarro died at twenty-six and Brown at twenty-five, which makes this a lineage of two men with about ten recorded years between them — and it is still the line every subsequent hard bop trumpeter works in.

In August 1951 police searched a parked car the two were sitting in and found narcotics presumed to be Powell's. Monk refused to testify against him, served sixty days, and had his cabaret card revoked.

It cost him six years of work in New York clubs, at exactly the point his writing was maturing. He did not get the card back until 1957, when the Five Spot residency immediately followed.
Evans called Powell the greatest influence on his playing, taking the right-hand line and then rebuilding the left hand into rootless voicings.
Silver's right hand comes straight out of Powell, with the fury replaced by a gospel bounce and a composer's economy.
Tyner started from Powell's percussive attack and then rebuilt the left hand around stacked fourths to suit Coltrane's modal frameworks.
Clarke made the first move of the pulse to the cymbal; Roach turned it into a complete system for playing melodically across the kit.
Blakey took Clarke's cymbal-led time and added a weight and volume that made the drums the loudest voice in the band rather than its floor.
Clarke was the Modern Jazz Quartet's original drummer, leaving for Paris before the group settled into the dinner-jacket formality it became known for.

The quintet they co-led from 1954 is the archetype of hard bop: a trumpeter of extraordinary evenness over a drummer composing underneath rather than keeping time.

Both were serious, disciplined men in a scene that was neither. When Brown was killed in a car crash in 1956 at twenty-five, Roach drank heavily for years and never assembled another group on the same terms.
Roach and Lincoln married in 1962 and worked together on the most explicitly political jazz records of the era before separating a decade later.
Roach's group gave Rollins the setting for Saxophone Colossus-era playing, with the drums answering his motivic development phrase for phrase.

The two founded Debut Records in 1952, an early attempt by musicians to own their own masters, and issued the Massey Hall concert with Parker, Gillespie and Powell on it.

In 1960 they staged a rival festival at Newport in protest at the main event's fees and programming. The partnership was between two difficult, politically explicit men who agreed almost entirely about the industry and often about nothing else.

The 1957 Five Spot residency is Coltrane's real education. Monk showed him how to move through unfamiliar harmony rather than around it, wrote out nothing, and would leave the stand mid-tune to let him work it out alone.

Coltrane described falling into an empty elevator shaft when he lost his place. He came out of it with the harmonic confidence that made Giant Steps possible eighteen months later.
Monk employed and coached the young Rollins, and Rollins has described being left to work out his own solution to the tunes rather than being shown one.
Taylor took Monk's percussive touch and deliberate dissonance as a starting point, then removed the song forms that had been holding them in place.
Hancock has described Monk's use of space and deliberately wrong notes as permission to leave things out, a lesson he applied in the Davis quintet.
Evans recorded Monk's tunes early and admired the compositional logic under the apparent awkwardness, which shaped how he voiced a melody.
Coltrane's first tenor model was Gordon's big Philadelphia-friendly sound, still audible in the early Prestige sessions before the harmonic density took over.
Johnson played and wrote for Davis's Blue Note and Prestige dates in the early fifties, one of the few trombonists Davis used at any length.
