From the Birth of the Cool nonet through Miles Ahead, Porgy and Bess and Sketches of Spain, Evans wrote settings that place a single exposed trumpet inside a shifting orchestral cloud.

Davis trusted him further than anyone, and Evans wrote specifically for the way Davis played — the small range, the flugelhorn tone, the silences. It is the longest and most equal composer-soloist partnership in postwar jazz, and both men treated it as the serious work.

Mulligan was part of the arranging circle that met in Evans's one-room basement flat behind a Chinese laundry, along with John Lewis, Lee Konitz and Davis.

He wrote several of the Birth of the Cool charts and helped fix the nonet's unusual instrumentation — French horn and tuba included — which is the instrumentation Evans then used for the rest of his career.
Konitz played the Birth of the Cool sessions and later Evans's own albums, his pale tone suiting writing built on blend rather than attack.

Schneider worked as Evans's assistant in the mid-eighties, copying and preparing scores and sitting in on the rehearsals, at a point when he was largely out of fashion.

What she took was a method rather than a manner: writing for the specific players in front of you and treating instrumental colour as the primary material. Her orchestra is the reason his approach survived as a living practice instead of a set of records to admire.
Davis hired Konitz for the 1949 nonet over objections that he should be using a Black alto player, and said flatly that he wanted that particular sound.
Lewis wrote and played on the Birth of the Cool sessions, part of the arranging circle that met in Gil Evans's basement apartment.
Their pianoless quartet of 1952 made both men famous, with baritone and trumpet weaving counterpoint where the chords would normally be stated.

Konitz studied with Tristano for years — singing solos before playing them, improvising over unfamiliar keys, drilling long lines with no accents to lean on.

He emerged with an alto sound almost nobody else had, pale and dry, and it was the one credible alternative to Parker's language rather than a variation on it. The teaching relationship is the clearest single case in jazz of a pedagogy producing an original voice.

Evans absorbed Tristano's insistence on long, evenly weighted lines and on hearing an idea completely before committing it to the keys.

What he did not take was the coolness — he replaced Tristano's deliberate flatness of affect with an impressionist harmony drawn from Debussy and Ravel. The Tristano school is the discipline underneath a style usually described purely in terms of feeling.
Desmond's floating alto against Brubeck's blocky, sometimes hammering piano is the whole tension of the quartet, and it held for seventeen years.
Columbia's backing let Brubeck release an album of odd metres in 1959, which the label expected to fail and which became the first jazz million-seller.
Corea's late-sixties stint with Getz gave him a working platform for the Latin-inflected writing he later took into Return to Forever.
The Modern Jazz Quartet ran for over forty years on the friction between Lewis's fugal restraint and Jackson's blues heat, in dinner jackets throughout.
The two recorded together on Blakey's earliest Blue Note dates, when the vibraphone was still a plausible front-line voice in the emerging hard bop sound.

The two co-led the original Jazz Messengers — Silver's gospel-inflected tunes and Blakey's press rolls, the two halves of what became hard bop.

The partnership ended in 1956 when Silver left and took most of the band with him. Blakey kept the name, and both men spent the next thirty years running versions of the same idea: a working group that developed young players and put their writing on record.
The Birdland sessions of 1954 with Brown and Silver are effectively the first hard bop records, made before the group had a settled name.
Morgan spent two long spells with the Messengers, and Blakey's press rolls under his solos are the setting in which his style hardened.

Shorter joined in 1959 and became the Messengers' musical director, which meant writing most of the book as well as playing it.

His tunes — Lester Left Town, Ping Pong — pushed the band past the soul-jazz formula that Moanin' had made profitable, and taught him how to write for a specific group of players. Miles Davis spent the next three years trying to hire him out of it.
The Messengers gave Hubbard a nightly platform for the brilliant, hard-edged tone he later carried into both free jazz and seventies crossover.
McLean's spell in the Messengers came exactly as his Parker inheritance was hardening into the sharper, more astringent voice that became his own.
Jarrett's brief 1966 stint was his first significant New York job, immediately before Charles Lloyd and then Miles Davis.

Marsalis joined in the summer of 1980, still a teenager and the last in a thirty-year line of young leaders finished in that band, and Blakey gave him a bandstand on which to be heard nightly.

What he took from it was less a style than a model: a working group as an institution that trains people. Jazz at Lincoln Center is the Messengers' method, scaled up, endowed, and given a building.
Blakey's press rolls under Silver's gospel-inflected piano set the rhythmic template the rest of hard bop worked from.

Lion founded the label in 1939 with almost no money, after a Carnegie Hall boogie-woogie concert convinced him the music was worth documenting properly.

His one structural innovation was paying musicians for rehearsal time before the session — the practical reason Blue Note records sound composed where their competitors sound assembled. He ran it with Francis Wolff, another German emigre, for nearly thirty years.

The Messengers' long Blue Note run gave the label its house sound and gave Blakey a permanent shop window for each new lineup he assembled.

Because Lion paid for rehearsal, the young players in the band arrived at their first recording sessions with the material already worked in — which is why so many Messengers debuts sound like the work of established leaders.
Silver spent nearly thirty years on the label, longer than any other artist, and his tunes supplied much of its house repertoire.
The Sidewinder's unexpected chart success in 1964 kept the label solvent and briefly convinced it that every session needed a boogaloo track.

Blue Note recorded Monk as a leader in 1947 when no one was buying, documenting the compositions years before the public accepted them.

Alfred Lion also paid Monk's back union dues while he was serving the sixty days that cost him his cabaret card, and compiled the old 78s into Genius of Modern Music while he was inside — the label functioning as a patron rather than a business.
Smith's late-fifties run effectively invented the organ trio record and gave the label a reliable seller well outside the jazz press.
Gordon's mid-sixties Blue Note albums, cut partly in New Jersey and partly in Europe during his years based in Copenhagen, are what kept his name alive in America.
Shorter's leader dates ran in parallel with his Miles Davis years and contain his strangest and most personal writing.
Hancock recorded for the label from the age of twenty-two, and Empyrean Isles and Maiden Voyage are where hard bop turns modal.
The label recorded Taylor twice in the mid-sixties, giving free jazz's least compromising pianist a properly engineered document at a point when nobody else would.

Black Radio was the label's flagship crossover of the 2010s, putting rappers and R&B singers on a Blue Note release as collaborators rather than guests.

It repeated a pattern the label had run before with Jimmy Smith's organ records and Cassandra Wilson's nineties albums: back a musician slightly ahead of the market and let the category catch up.
Van Gelder engineered nearly the whole classic Blue Note catalogue, first in his parents' living room in Hackensack and then at Englewood Cliffs.
Van Gelder recorded Coltrane for Prestige, Blue Note and Impulse, and the sound of A Love Supreme, close and dry with no studio wash, is his.
Van Gelder engineered Saxophone Colossus and the Blue Note quartet dates, miking the tenor close enough that the reed itself is audible.
Morgan was Brown's most obvious inheritor in Philadelphia, and took over the succession when Brown died in 1956.
Hubbard inherited Brown's combination of speed and full tone, and recorded memorial programmes of his material.

Hancock's first significant work was in Silver's band, and Watermelon Man is written straight out of the funky-tune tradition Silver had established.

The lesson was commercial as much as musical: that a jazz tune could carry a hook without thinning its harmony, and that writing your own repertoire is what keeps a leader solvent. Hancock has applied it in every idiom he has worked in since.

Through the mid-fifties the two were treated as competing claimants to the tenor chair, though they were friendly and recorded together on Tenor Madness.

Each withdrew from performance at points partly in response to the other's advances.
A Night at the Village Vanguard catches Rollins working without a piano, which exposes how much of the harmony he was carrying alone.
The 1961 Vanguard recordings, with Dolphy sitting in, are where Coltrane's playing first broke openly with conventional form in front of a paying audience.
Sunday at the Village Vanguard captures the Evans trio days before Scott LaFaro's death, and is the standard example of a trio playing as three equal voices.
Mingus used the room for long residencies where the music was rehearsed in front of the paying audience, arguments included.
Her orchestra held a long-running Monday night residency at the club, where most of its repertoire was first tested in public.
Rollins recorded repeatedly with Davis in the early fifties and wrote Oleo, Doxy and Airegin for those sessions.

Adderley's blues warmth against Coltrane's density gave the Kind of Blue sextet its two-sided front line, and Davis played on Adderley's Somethin' Else in return, the only leader date of another musician's he appeared on in those years.
Zawinul spent nine years in Adderley's quintet and wrote Mercy, Mercy, Mercy for it, his first hit and his first experiment with electric keyboard texture.
Their two Verve albums together are the meeting point of the organ trio and the jazz guitar tradition, both at their commercial peak.
Metheny learned Montgomery's solos as a teenager in Missouri and has described the octave technique and the round tone as his first musical grammar.
Hubbard played on Free Jazz, one of several mainstream players Coleman drafted to prove his approach was not a lack of technique.
Shorter's arrival in 1964 completed the second great quintet and gave Davis a composer whose tunes left the harmony deliberately unresolved.

Shorter co-founded the band in 1970 having just left Miles Davis, and then spent sixteen years largely refusing to be its star soloist.

He wrote less than Zawinul and played fewer choruses than his reputation warranted, on the stated principle that the band was the instrument. It cost him a decade of critical standing and produced the most influential ensemble sound of the seventies.

Zawinul came out of Cannonball Adderley's band with a hit and a growing interest in synthesisers, and made the layered electronic surface the group's identity.

His writing pulled it from abstract collective texture toward tight electric funk, which is where the audience arrived and where the arguments with critics began. Heavy Weather is his record more than anyone's.

Pastorius introduced himself to Zawinul after a show as the greatest bass player in the world, and was hired within the year.

He turned the fretless electric bass into a lead voice, wrote for the band, and briefly co-produced it into a commercial force. He also destabilised it: the volume, the showmanship and eventually the illness made the arrangement unsustainable, and both parties knew it.
Their partnership ran from Weather Report's founding to its end, an unusual case of two established leaders agreeing to share one band's identity.

Davis hired Coltrane in 1955 as an unproven player, fired him for unreliability, rehired him after Monk had straightened him out, and then handed him the modal frameworks of Milestones and Kind of Blue.

He complained constantly about the length of the solos and kept the band together anyway. Everything Coltrane did afterwards starts from the space Davis gave him and the harmony Davis took away.

Evans was in the band for eight months and shaped Kind of Blue more than anyone but Davis — the harmonic conception, the voicings, the sketch that became Blue in Green.

He left partly because touring with the sextet as its only white member was made unpleasant for him nightly. Davis brought him back specially for the session, which is the measure of what he thought the piano chair required.
Chambers was the constant through the quintet, the sextet and Kind of Blue, holding the harmony steady while everything above it was rebuilt.
Davis said the band's sound depended on Jones, and kept rehiring him despite the unreliability that came with his addiction.
With Red Garland the two formed the first great Davis rhythm section, elastic enough to swing hard while leaving the trumpet almost naked.

Hancock spent five years in the second quintet learning to play less — Davis's instruction was usually to leave the obvious chord out and let the horn imply it.

With Carter and Williams he formed a rhythm section that could shift the harmonic ground mid-phrase, the most interactive unit in the music. Davis later pushed him toward the Fender Rhodes he had no wish to play, and the whole electric career follows from it.
Williams was seventeen when he joined, and his willingness to abandon the stated beat is what let the quintet play time as a shared negotiation.
Carter anchored the second quintet for five years, choosing notes that redirected the harmony rather than confirming it.
Hancock, Carter and Williams functioned as a single instrument in the second quintet, capable of changing the harmonic ground under a soloist mid-phrase.
Bass and drums functioned in the second quintet as one elastic unit, able to double, halve or suspend the tempo without a word being said.
Corea played electric piano on Bitches Brew under instruction to stop voicing chords conventionally, which pushed him into an abstraction he later moved away from.
Jarrett played electric keyboards for Davis for two years while openly loathing the instruments, and used the exposure to build an acoustic career.
McLaughlin arrived from London and was recording with Davis within days, and his distorted guitar is the loudest single element in the Bitches Brew sessions.
Zawinul wrote In a Silent Way, and Davis stripped his arrangement back to a drone, which set the pattern for the whole electric period.
Columbia's advances funded orchestral projects and long studio time no independent could match, and kept Davis in the mainstream press for three decades.

Macero recorded hours of unstructured playing and assembled finished pieces afterwards with a razor blade — loops, repeats and splices that no one had performed as a sequence.

Davis tolerated the method, then relied on it, and never fully acknowledged it. In a Silent Way and Bitches Brew are editing jobs as much as performances, which makes Macero the closest thing jazz has to a producer as co-author.
Macero produced Mingus Ah Um for Columbia and cut several tracks down to fit the record, edits Mingus never accepted.
Columbia carried Ellington through his mid-century revival, including the 1956 Newport recording that put him back on magazine covers.
Columbia marketed Marsalis simultaneously as a classical and a jazz artist in the early eighties, which gave his traditionalist argument unusual reach.

Marsalis attacked the electric period as a commercial surrender and a betrayal of the tradition; Davis dismissed him in return as a gifted young man playing museum music.

The exchange, conducted in interviews through the eighties and once awkwardly on stage at Vancouver, framed the decade's argument about what jazz is for — a living process or an inheritance to be curated. Both positions have institutions built on them now.
Tyner's fourth-based voicings gave the quartet a harmonic floor stable enough for Coltrane to leave the chords entirely and still be heard as playing something.

Jones surrounded Coltrane in overlapping triplet waves rather than stating a beat, which is what made the quartet's freedom structurally possible.

Their duets are the most sustained two-man exchange in the recorded music, each pushing the other past the point of comfort for twenty minutes at a time. Jones left in 1966 when a second drummer was added and he could no longer hear what he was doing.
Garrison joined in 1961 and stayed to the end, the only member of the quartet who followed Coltrane all the way into the late free playing.
The two held the quartet's centre for four years, and both left when Coltrane added a second drummer and abandoned fixed harmony.
Garrison's insistent pedal figures gave Jones licence to abandon the stated beat entirely, since the ground was already being held.

They married in the mid-sixties, and she replaced McCoy Tyner in the band in 1966 — wife and pianist at once, in a group most of the audience had already stopped following.

After his death at forty she inherited the catalogue, the players and the devotional direction, and took it somewhere he had not: harp, strings, Indian liturgy, eventually an ashram. It is the rarest kind of jazz partnership, one that continued after one party was gone.
She replaced McCoy Tyner in 1966, and her sweeping arpeggios suited a band that no longer wanted a fixed harmonic floor under it.

Dolphy's presence in the 1961 band drew the anti-jazz reviews that made both men defend the music in print.

His leaping intervals gave Coltrane a partner willing to go further out than the quartet alone would.
Coltrane pushed Impulse to record Shepp and put him on the Ascension session, effectively using his commercial standing to fund the players behind him.
Ayler's overtone-shredded tone and folk-hymn material pointed Coltrane's last two years further from measured form than the quartet had gone.
Impulse gave Coltrane artistic control and a large budget from 1961, and marketed itself afterwards as the house that Trane built.
Shepp's Impulse albums, several of them explicitly political, were effectively underwritten by Coltrane's commercial standing at the label.
Impulse signed Ayler at Coltrane's urging, then pushed him toward vocals and rock rhythms in search of sales that never came.
Her Impulse albums put harp, strings and Indian devotional structure into a jazz catalogue, and were largely ignored until their rediscovery decades later.
The Black Saint and the Sinner Lady, cut for Impulse in 1963, is his most ambitious single work and was assembled with heavy studio editing.

Washington's large-scale spiritual jazz — choir, strings, a tenor at the centre — takes its ambition and its framing directly from the last Coltrane period.

What he leaves behind is the abrasiveness: the scale is Ascension's, the surface is closer to Alice Coltrane's or Pharoah Sanders's. That the model reached a hip-hop audience fifty years later is the clearest evidence of how far that music travelled.

Her Impulse records — harp, strings, drone, Indian liturgical structure — are the model for the scale and the spiritual framing of the Los Angeles scene Washington leads.

She spent her later life running an ashram in California and recording for its community, which put the music physically in the city that produced Washington's generation. They inherited a local tradition as much as a discography.
The Arkestra's use of choir, costume and cosmology as part of the music rather than decoration is a precedent Washington's large ensembles draw on openly.
Cherry's pocket trumpet shadowed Coleman's alto through the 1959-61 quartets, playing heads in loose unison and then diverging without a chord sequence to return to.
Coltrane took lessons from Coleman and hired his rhythm section for The Avant-Garde, which is as direct an acknowledgement as one leader ever gave another.
Coleman's example showed Shepp that a saxophonist could keep blues phrasing intact while discarding the chord sequence underneath it.
Song X put Metheny's audience in front of Coleman's harmolodics, and remains the most abrasive record either man released.
The two arrived at free playing from opposite ends, Coleman from blues melody and Taylor from the conservatory, and were persistently set against each other by critics.
The Avant-Garde put Cherry beside Coltrane on Coleman's own tunes, using Coleman's bassist and drummer, and is the clearest evidence of how seriously Coltrane took that music.

Dolphy was the voice Mingus wrote his most demanding parts for, on alto, flute and bass clarinet, and the one player he never shouted down.

The European tapes of 1964 catch the two arguing musically in real time, Dolphy going further out than the material asks and Mingus following him. Dolphy died months later at thirty-six of undiagnosed diabetes, and Mingus wrote about the loss for years.
McLean's spell in the Jazz Workshop meant learning parts by ear at the piano and being shouted at from the bandstand, a method he wrote about afterwards.
Pastorius played on Three or Four Shades of Blues, Mingus's last major album, at a point when illness had ended Mingus's own playing.

Spalding takes from Mingus the idea of the bassist as composer and bandleader rather than accompanist, and has performed and reworked his material extensively.

The inheritance is also one of scope: writing that mixes song, protest and autobiography without deciding in advance which register it belongs in.
Williams grew up studying Jones's crispness and rimshot placement, then dismantled the steady beat those techniques existed to serve.
Hancock joined the Davis band after Evans had already redefined what its piano chair meant, and inherited rootless voicings as standard equipment.
Jarrett inherited Evans's touch and his conception of the trio as a three-way conversation, then extended both into hour-long improvised forms.
Mehldau's trio works in the lineage Evans established, though he replaced the impressionist harmony with contrapuntal left-hand independence.
The two toured as an acoustic piano duo in 1978 and repeatedly afterwards, having taken the same electric route out of the Davis bands.

Glasper treats Hancock's movement between jazz harmony and Black popular music as the precedent that makes his own work legible rather than a compromise.

The two have recorded together, and the argument Hancock had to fight in 1973 over Head Hunters is the same one Glasper faced over Black Radio — with the difference that Hancock had already won it.
Lifetime, with Williams, McLaughlin and Larry Young, was louder and rougher than anything Davis released, and largely ignored at the time.
Mehldau's long-form solo playing works in the territory Jarrett opened, with more explicit classical counterpoint and less gospel.
The two recorded together in 2006, pairing Metheny's melodic writing with Mehldau's denser harmonic reading of it.

Pastorius established the electric bass as a singing lead voice, which is the tradition Spalding plays and sings inside rather than around.

What she adds is the voice itself: the technical problem she solved — improvising vocally while playing an independent bass line — only makes sense in a lineage where the bass had already stopped accompanying.

Lincoln took from Holiday the principle that a jazz singer could state something unbearable plainly, without dressing it as entertainment.

Holiday's insistence on keeping Strange Fruit in her act is the direct precedent for the openly political work Lincoln made with Max Roach twenty years later.
Carter took Holiday's freedom with the beat considerably further, stretching a lyric until the written melody is only implied.

Granz managed Fitzgerald for decades and founded Verve substantially to record her, then conceived the Songbook series that canonised the American popular songwriters.

He also wrote non-segregation clauses into her touring contracts and cancelled dates that broke them. It is the most productive artist-manager relationship in jazz, and one of the few where the businessman's convictions cost him money on purpose.
Granz recorded Holiday's late Verve sessions, catching a damaged voice with the phrasing intact and first-rate players behind it.
Basie's Clef and Verve years under Granz produced the small-group sessions that sit alongside the big band in his catalogue.
The two were constantly compared and occasionally billed together, Fitzgerald prized for clarity and swing, Vaughan for range and harmonic daring.

Carter's model was the singer as improvising instrumentalist and bandleader who hires and trains her own young rhythm section, then lets them leave.

Spalding works from exactly that template, and from Carter's refusal of the standards-and-strings formula that the industry offered every woman who could sing in tune.
The two recorded and broadcast together in the fifties, crossing from jazz into a mainstream pop audience at roughly the same moment and paying different prices for it.

Marsalis built the programme from a summer concert series into a permanent orchestra with a repertory mission and eventually its own purpose-built hall.

It gave jazz the institutional footing that classical music has had for a century, and it did so by making choices — which composers, which decades, which definition — that musicians have argued with ever since. Both the achievement and the argument are his.
They have appeared on each other's records, part of a generation that moves between jazz, R&B and hip-hop without treating the borders as real.

Both played on Kendrick Lamar's To Pimp a Butterfly, the record that put contemporary jazz musicians in front of a mass hip-hop audience without labelling them as jazz.

They work the same territory from opposite ends — Washington through large-ensemble spiritual jazz, Glasper through production and keyboard texture — and the crossover neither had to argue for is the thing their predecessors spent thirty years fighting about.
Her orchestra has been commissioned and presented by the programme, one of the few contemporary composers regularly in its concert seasons.

Columbia paired its two biggest Black artists across three 1925 sessions for nine sides, beginning with St. Louis Blues on 14 January. Smith sings the line and Armstrong answers each phrase on cornet, neither deferring to the other.

The records fix the relationship between blues voice and jazz horn that the rest of the century worked from. By most accounts the session was cordial and competitive rather than warm — Smith did not much like being answered back.

Holiday said she wanted Bessie Smith's big sound and Louis Armstrong's feeling, and took from Smith the refusal to prettify a lyric or apologise for its content.

What she did not take was the volume: Holiday worked with a small voice at close range where Smith filled a tent without amplification. The inheritance is in the material as much as the technique — the licence to sing about hard things directly, which is what let her take on Strange Fruit.
Wilson works in the low, unhurried register Smith established, and has recorded her material as blues rather than as jazz repertory.
Smith was Columbia's biggest-selling artist of the 1920s, and the money her records made helped keep the label solvent through the decade.
Smith played the Harlem theatres on the circuit that the Apollo came to dominate, at the tail of her career as the blues craze receded.
Ory hired the teenage Armstrong to replace King Oliver in his New Orleans band, the first significant job Armstrong held.
Ory's trombone is the countermelody running under the Red Hot Peppers sides, the clearest surviving example of tailgate playing in an arranged setting.

Ory and Oliver led competing New Orleans bands whose personnel moved constantly between them, and for a while Oliver played cornet in Ory's group.

When Oliver left for Chicago, Ory hired the teenage Louis Armstrong to replace him — so the same chair, in the same city, passed from one to the next. Both men ended up recording versions of the same New Orleans ensemble style a thousand miles apart.
Powell took Tatum's harmonic substitutions and speed and stripped the ornamentation away, leaving the line bare.

Parker washed dishes at Jimmy's Chicken Shack in Harlem where Tatum was playing nightly, and heard him for months on end at close range.

What he took was the harmonic apparatus: Tatum's passing chords, substitutions and upper-interval runs, transferred from a solo piano context onto an alto in a rhythm section. Bebop's harmony is Tatum's, redistributed among five players.
Tatum came out of the stride tradition Waller popularised, and Waller reportedly announced from the stand that God had entered the room when Tatum walked in.
The two defined the poles of thirties piano, Tatum overwhelming and Wilson poised, and each was measured against the other in the press.
Granz recorded Tatum's complete solo and group masterpieces in the fifties, a systematic documentation project no one else attempted.

Wilson led and organised the 1935-39 studio sessions that produced Holiday's finest records, hiring the players — Lester Young among them — and keeping the arrangements to a head and a running order.

The material was often whatever song plugging had left over that week, and the method turned it into the best-loved small-group jazz of the decade. His piano introductions are the frame that lets her enter late and behind the beat.
Wilson's place in the Goodman trio from 1936 put a Black musician on stage with a white band nightly, at real commercial risk to Goodman.
Carter's charts for Henderson helped establish how saxophone sections voice a chord, a convention every big band afterwards inherited.
The two came up together in Henderson's band and later recorded in Europe as equals, one on alto and one on tenor.
Parker admired Carter's alto sound and fluency, and it is Carter rather than Johnny Hodges who sits behind his tone.
Granz recorded Carter extensively and used him as an arranger for Verve sessions, keeping him working through the lean years for swing players.

Calloway ran a lucrative, well-drilled orchestra and had no patience for the harmonic experiments Gillespie was smuggling into it, calling them Chinese music.

The relationship ended in 1941 when a spitball landed on stage, Calloway blamed Gillespie, and the argument became a knife fight backstage. Both told the story as comedy afterwards; at the time it cost Gillespie the best-paid job of his early career.
Calloway's orchestra took over the Cotton Club residency when Ellington left, and its broadcasts made him a national name.
Two Cotton Club orchestras selling very different things to the same audience: Calloway's showmanship against Ellington's composition.
Fitzgerald won the Apollo amateur night in 1934 at seventeen, having intended to dance, and was hired out of it within months.
Vaughan won the same amateur night in 1942, which led directly to her job with Earl Hines.
Holiday played the Apollo repeatedly through her career, in front of the audience least willing to accept a mannered performance.
The Basie band was a regular headline attraction, and the theatre's stage schedule shaped how the swing bands toured.
Stitt was told all his life that he was imitating Parker, and answered that he had been playing that way before hearing him — a claim Parker himself seems to have accepted.
Stitt played in Gillespie's groups in the mid-forties, the setting where the comparison with Parker first became unavoidable.
Both were competitive tenor duellists who built reputations on cutting contests, and their meetings on record are structured as combat.

Gillespie hired Pozo in 1947 on Mario Bauzá's recommendation and put a Cuban ritual drummer, who spoke almost no English, at the front of an American jazz orchestra.

Manteca and Cubana Be, Cubana Bop set genuine rumba drumming against bebop harmony rather than borrowing a Latin flavour. Pozo was shot dead in a Harlem bar a year later, having permanently enlarged what jazz rhythm could contain.
The principle Pozo established, that percussion could be a compositional layer rather than timekeeping, runs directly into the electric bands of the seventies.

Pettiford took the Ellington bass chair in 1945, three years after Jimmy Blanton's death had left the orchestra without the bassist who had redefined the instrument, and carried Blanton's innovations into bebop.
Two bassists of the same generation who both pushed the instrument toward solo status and both wrote for their own bands, with a rivalry neither hid.
Pettiford was on Monk's Blue Note sessions and among the few bassists comfortable with tunes that refuse to resolve where the ear expects.
Pettiford was part of the house circle at Minton's, supplying the bass line that made the new harmonic substitutions audible.

Davis carried Jamal's records around, told his rhythm section to study them, and instructed Red Garland to play Jamal's voicings outright.

What he wanted was the discipline of leaving things out: vamps instead of continuous soloing, dynamics instead of volume, silence used structurally. He recorded several tunes from Jamal's book, and the whole open surface of the first quintet comes out of it.

Garland was hired into the first Miles Davis quintet partly for his ability to reproduce Jamal's touch and block chords on demand, and Davis said so openly.

It is an unusually literal transmission: one pianist instructed to sound like another, in a band whose whole surface then depended on it. Garland's own contribution was to make the borrowed manner swing harder than the original.
Glasper cites Jamal's vamps and negative space as an early model for building a groove that leaves room for another voice.
Mobley was in the original Jazz Messengers front line, and his soft-toned unhurried phrasing is the counterweight to Blakey's volume.
Mobley took the tenor chair after Coltrane left, a job that meant nightly comparison with a predecessor Davis openly preferred.
Mobley inherited the Davis tenor chair in 1961, holding the least enviable seat in jazz for two years.
Shorter finally took the chair in 1964 after Davis had spent three years trying to replace Coltrane.
Mobley made more albums for Blue Note than almost anyone, and Soul Station is the label's most quietly admired tenor record.
Green recorded prolifically for the label in the sixties, much of it unissued at the time and reissued decades later to a wholly different audience.
Benson took Green's single-line clarity as a starting point before adding the technique and the singing that made him a pop act.
Green was the guitarist on many of the organ dates that defined the format, playing lines that leave room for the Hammond's sustain.
Byrd passed through the Messengers in the mid-fifties, one of the earliest of Blakey's graduates to become a leader.

Byrd gave Hancock his first steady New York job, put him up in his apartment, and pressed Blue Note into signing him as a leader at twenty-two.

He also told him to keep the publishing on his own tunes — practical advice that made Watermelon Man pay for years. It is the least glamorous kind of mentorship and one of the most consequential in the label's history.
Byrd's long Blue Note run ended with the gospel-choir and funk records that the jazz press disowned and the label's accountants did not.
Timmons wrote Moanin' for the Messengers, the tune that made the band commercially viable and defined the soul jazz idiom.
Timmons moved to Adderley's quintet and wrote This Here for it, repeating the trick that had worked for Blakey.
Riverside recorded Timmons as a leader off the back of two hits he had written for other people's bands.

Henderson joined Silver's quintet for Song for My Father in 1964, and his solo on the title track is the most quoted tenor chorus of the period.

Silver wrote tunes with an internal logic that rewarded a thematic improviser, which suited Henderson exactly — dry, angular and unhurried against a bassline everyone in the room already knew.
Henderson's Blue Note albums are the label's clearest bridge between hard bop discipline and the freer playing arriving around it.
Two tenor players of the same age on the same label, arriving at oblique harmony from opposite directions and often set against each other by critics.
Brecker took Henderson's angular intervallic vocabulary and drove it through a much more aggressive and technically extreme delivery.
Garland's light block chords gave the first quintet its unhurried surface, and Davis kept close control over exactly how much he played.
With Philly Joe Jones, the two formed the rhythm section that made the first quintet's relaxed tempo possible.
Evans replaced Garland in 1958, swapping a blues-rooted swing feel for the impressionist harmony that made Kind of Blue possible.
Cobb is the only drummer on Kind of Blue, and his brushwork sets the session's whole temperature.
Cobb took the drum chair when Jones's unreliability finally exhausted Davis's patience, bringing a quieter and steadier presence.
Chambers and Cobb held the sextet together through Kind of Blue and the touring that followed it.
Carter took the bass chair in 1963, replacing a player whose sound had defined the band for eight years.
LaFaro was hired into a trio that Evans intended as three equal voices, and he took the invitation further than anyone had before.
Bass and drums in the Evans trio abandoned their supporting roles simultaneously, which is why the group still sounds unusual.
LaFaro played on Free Jazz and in Coleman's groups, one of the few bassists able to work with and without a chord sequence equally well.

LaFaro established in the Bill Evans trio that a bassist could interrupt, carry melody and decline to walk; Pastorius took that claim onto the electric instrument and made it permanent.

Both died young, both left a small recorded body of work, and both are the reason bass players are now expected to be soloists rather than furniture.
Motian's brushed, implied time in the trio was the first widely heard example of a drummer stating almost nothing and still holding a band.
Motian anchored Jarrett's American quartet through the seventies, a band far rougher and more folk-inflected than the later European work.
Sanders joined in 1965 and matched the leader scream for scream, which is the point at which much of Coltrane's audience left.
Sanders played on her Impulse albums, supplying the ecstatic tenor against her harp and strings on Journey in Satchidananda.
Karma, and its side-long The Creator Has a Master Plan, became the label's most enduring statement of spiritual jazz after Coltrane's death.
Sanders's late modal calm, long vamps under an unhurried tenor, is the closest precedent for the Los Angeles spiritual jazz revival.
Braxton came up inside the AACM's Chicago school, which taught composition and self-presentation alongside playing and left him a systematiser for life.
Sun Ra's Chicago years established the local precedent for a self-organised Black experimental collective with its own rules and its own economy.
Taylor's demonstration that a jazz musician could work at the density of contemporary composition opened the ground Braxton then mapped formally.
Iyer inherits Braxton's insistence that rigorous theory and improvisation are one activity rather than two that must be reconciled.
DeJohnette drummed on Bitches Brew and the live electric bands, holding a rock backbeat and a jazz cymbal line at the same time.
With Gary Peacock, DeJohnette and Jarrett ran the standards trio for thirty years, an unusually long-lived working group.
DeJohnette's own ECM albums as a leader are the least discussed part of a career spent making other people's bands work.
Two drummers of the same generation who each solved the problem of playing rock volume without abandoning jazz interaction, by different routes.
Brecker absorbed the whole Coltrane harmonic apparatus and then applied it to pop sessions, which made it the default tenor language of the eighties.
80/81 put Brecker in an open, largely free setting that his session reputation had obscured, and he treated it as the record he wanted to be judged on.
Benson was the most convincing of Montgomery's inheritors, and followed him into a crossover career that drew the same complaints.
The label's willingness to release an unedited solo concert made The Köln Concert possible, and its success funded a great deal else.
Metheny's early ECM records established the bright, open sound that made him the most commercially successful jazz guitarist of his generation.
Corea's ECM solo and Return to Forever debut records are the acoustic hinge between his Miles Davis years and the electric band that followed.
Jarrett took the keyboard chair in Davis's band directly from Corea, and for a period the two played in it together.
Shorter was Davis's target as Coltrane's replacement from the moment Coltrane left, and it took three years and two other tenors to get him.
Two members of the same quintet who left it in the same direction, and have recorded as a duo repeatedly since.
She took the piano chair when Tyner left, a change that removed the quartet's last fixed harmonic anchor.
Fitzgerald took over the orchestra on Webb's death in 1939 and fronted it for three years, an almost unheard-of position for a woman of twenty-two.

McRae wrote Dream of Life as a teenager and Holiday recorded it in 1939, which was McRae's first professional recognition; she was then the intermission pianist at Minton's.

She called Holiday her primary influence and spent the rest of her career refusing to imitate her, recording a Holiday tribute album on her own dry, ironic terms.
Carmen Sings Monk set lyrics to his tunes and proved they worked as songs, something the composer's reputation for angularity had obscured.

Close friends and constant comparisons: Vaughan with the instrument and the range, McRae with the dry ironic reading of a lyric.

They recorded together late, sniping affectionately across the microphone, and each was clear about what the other had that she did not. It is the rare documented case of two singers treating the rivalry as a joke they were both in on.
Wilson's Blue Note albums in the nineties gave the label its biggest vocal success since its revival and redefined what a jazz vocal record could contain.
Two singers a generation apart who both refused the standards-and-strings formula and ran their own bands to avoid it.
The four albums Davis cut in two 1956 marathon sessions to end his Prestige contract are among the best-loved records of the decade, made under conditions designed to be cheap.
Coltrane's Prestige years document him practising in public, the harmonic density thickening from session to session.
Saxophone Colossus was a Prestige date, cut fast and with almost no rehearsal, which is the label's method at its most successful.
Van Gelder engineered for Prestige and Blue Note simultaneously, which is why records from rival labels share a sound.
Riverside started Monk on albums of Ellington and standards to establish him as a pianist before letting him record his own repertoire, and the strategy worked.
The Evans trio's Riverside albums, including the Vanguard sessions, are the label's most enduring legacy.
Montgomery's Riverside period is the straight-ahead jazz side of a career that later turned toward orchestrated pop.
Adderley's Riverside quintet records are where soul jazz became a commercial category rather than a description.

The 1957 residency ran for months in a small Bowery bar and turned Monk from a cult figure with a revoked cabaret card into a critical necessity.

He had the room, the quartet with Coltrane, and finally an audience that came to listen rather than dance. The Five Spot's willingness to give a difficult pianist a long booking is the direct reason his repertoire entered general circulation.

Coleman's November 1959 opening, with Don Cherry, Charlie Haden and Billy Higgins, split the New York jazz world within a fortnight.

Established musicians came nightly to denounce or defend him from the same bar — Mingus ambivalent, Roach reportedly furious, Leonard Bernstein enthusiastic. Nothing about the music had changed since Los Angeles; what changed was that a small Bowery room let it be heard for months on end.
Taylor's residency at the club in the mid-fifties was among the first sustained public hearings for free playing in New York.
The 1961 Five Spot recordings with Booker Little are the fullest surviving document of Dolphy as a leader.
The 1956 performance, and Paul Gonsalves's twenty-seven choruses on Diminuendo and Crescendo in Blue, restarted Ellington's career in a single night.
Davis's 1955 appearance was the performance that persuaded Columbia to sign him and the critics to reconsider him.

Roach and Mingus staged a rival festival at Cliff Walk Manor in 1960, in protest at Newport's fees and its programming, and drew away a good part of the main event's musicians.

Roach also interrupted the official festival's stage in person that year. The quarrel was about who the festival economy was actually for, and both men made it in public rather than in private.
McBride became the festival's artistic director, putting a working bassist in charge of the institution musicians had spent decades arguing with.
Branford joined the Messengers alongside his brother, the last generation to be finished in that band.

Brothers who came up together in New Orleans and then in Art Blakey's band, Branford joining a year after Wynton and overlapping with him there, then split publicly over how strictly the tradition should be policed.

Branford toured with Sting, played the Tonight Show and took precisely the pop work Wynton had defined himself against; Wynton called it a betrayal in print. They have since recorded together repeatedly, which suggests the argument was always more public than private.
Columbia signed both brothers in the early eighties as part of the young-lions marketing push that reshaped the jazz market.
Iyer's ECM records place his rhythmic research in the label's spacious acoustic, which has helped carry it beyond a specialist audience.
Two pianists of the same generation drawing on hip-hop from opposite ends, one through rhythmic theory and one through production.
McBride works in the line Carter established of the bass as a lead melodic instrument with a full, singing tone.
McBride has led large ensembles performing Mingus's writing, treating him as the model of the bassist-composer.

McRae married Clarke in the mid-forties and recorded under the name Carmen Clarke, including her first sides as a pianist with Mercer Ellington's band.

They met at Minton's, where she was the intermission pianist and he was running the house band, and they later divorced. It is the one direct marital link between the bebop rhythm section and the singers who came out of the same room.
McRae won an Apollo amateur contest as a teenager, the same route into the profession that Fitzgerald and Vaughan took, and the one reliable audition available to a Black singer without connections.
Kitchings was married to Wilson during the years he was running the Billie Holiday sessions, which is how her songs reached Holiday in the first place.
Kitchings wrote Some Other Spring and Ghost of Yesterday, two of the harmonically richest songs Holiday recorded and among the few written specifically with her voice in mind.

Kitchings took the teenage McRae up, encouraged her to write, and introduced her to Holiday — the introduction that led to Holiday recording McRae's Dream of Life in 1939.

It is a chain of women mentoring each other across two generations that runs entirely outside the bandstand economy the men were operating in.

Shaw hired Holiday in 1938, making her one of the first Black singers to tour with an all-white orchestra, and then spent the engagement fighting hotels and sponsors over where she could enter, eat and wait.

She left within the year. Both told the story afterwards as evidence that the industry's racial arrangements could not be fixed by a bandleader's good intentions, however genuine.

Eldridge joined Shaw's band in 1944 and was refused entry at venues his own orchestra was headlining, an experience he described later in unusually plain terms.

Shaw had already been through the same thing with Holiday six years earlier and hired him anyway.
The two competing clarinettist-bandleaders of the swing era, endlessly compared, with Goodman the disciplinarian and Shaw the reluctant star who kept dissolving his own successful bands.

She drove him to gigs, paid his bills, took the charge when police found narcotics in her car in Delaware in 1958, and gave him a home in Weehawken for the last decade of his life when he had stopped playing.

Monk wrote Pannonica for her. The relationship has been endlessly speculated about and was, by every account of the people around them, a friendship and a patronage rather than an affair.

Parker collapsed at her suite in the Stanhope Hotel in March 1955 and died there, which cost her the tenancy and made her briefly notorious in the press.

She had known him only a short time; the scandal fixed her public reputation as the jazz baroness for the next forty years.
She supported Powell through his worst years, in Paris and then New York, at a point when his health made steady work impossible.
Lundvall ran Columbia's jazz operation at the turn of the eighties and used a major label's resources to build the young-lions roster around Wynton Marsalis.
Lundvall relaunched the dormant Blue Note in 1984 and ran it until 2010, restoring both the catalogue and the label's habit of signing musicians ahead of the market.

Lundvall signed Marsalis to Columbia in 1980, at nineteen and with one Blakey record behind him, and marketed him simultaneously as a jazz and a classical artist.

That contract is what gave the traditionalist argument a major label's distribution behind it.
Wilson's Blue Note signing under Lundvall produced the label's biggest vocal success of the nineties, on records that abandoned the standards repertoire almost entirely.
Bauzá was Calloway's musical director and the man who got Dizzy Gillespie into the orchestra — and who was still there when the spitball incident got him thrown out of it.

Bauzá brought Gillespie into Cab Calloway's band, taught him what Cuban rhythm actually consisted of rather than how it sounded from outside, and then handed him Chano Pozo.

Almost everything Gillespie did with Afro-Cuban music runs through this one relationship, and Gillespie said so for the rest of his life.
Bauzá knew Pozo from Havana and recommended him to Gillespie in 1947, the introduction that produced Manteca and put a rumbero in an American jazz orchestra.

Having taken Ory's cornet chair in New Orleans twenty years earlier, Armstrong sent for him in 1925 to play trombone in the Hot Five — the relationship reversed, with the pupil now hiring the man who had first employed him.

Ory's tailgate lines are the countermelody on the most important records in early jazz, and he was simultaneously recording with Oliver and Morton, the busiest trombonist in Chicago.
Monk recorded for Prestige between the Blue Note and Riverside years, at his lowest commercial point, with no cabaret card and almost no live work available to him.
